speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Prime Minister. Has the Prime Minister received any communication from the province of Saskatchewan that would indicate any change in the responsibilities which that province has already accepted with regard to the building of the South Saskatchewan dam? Further, what action is this government taking to meet with the province of Saskatchewan to discuss an early start on the dam construction project, as promised by the Prime Minister during the course of the election campaign?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as far as the promise to proceed with the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam is concerned, that promise will be carried out just as soon as the province of Saskatchewan and the federal government have arrived at a decision as to the distribution of financial responsibility for the construction work. I hope that at an early date a meeting can be arranged.
As far as the practicability of the scheme is concerned, and its feasibility, we believe that has been determined. There is no need to convince the members of this government and of this party as to feasibility and practicability. All that remains is to reach an agreement as to the division of responsibility, and I hope that steps to achieve that agreement will be taken at the earliest possible date.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the responsibility for the welfare of immigrants during the first 12 months after their admission to Canada is discharged by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker, in that regard. I wonder if the minister would tell us whether or not the government has made arrangements to accept another group of Hungarian refugees from Yugoslavia. If so, how many, and have arrangements been made to provide a thorough medical examination on their entry into this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Acting Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. gentleman raised the question. I had intended to follow up my previous remarks immediately with a reference to that matter.
It has been decided to admit 700 Hungarian refugees from Yugoslavia.	The United
Nations high commissioner for refugees visited Ottawa early in October and made representations to us, as he told us he was doing to all other countries which he felt would be in a position to receive these refugees. There were at that time some 4,800 Hungarian refugees in Yugoslavia who had indicated they would wish to emigrate, and we have been informed that there is virtually no winter accommodation for them in that country, with the result that if countries in a position to receive them did not do so the fact would be that these men and women would face the most desperate hardship in Yugoslavia during the winter months.

Accordingly the Canadian government agreed to receive 700 of those who are in the refugee camps in Yugoslavia.
I have a table, Mr. Speaker, showing the number of these refugees in Yugoslavia which various countries have agreed to take, and with the 700 now agreed to be received by Canada the total we will have taken from Yugoslavia will be 1,779. In order to select and process these refugees we are sending an immigration team to Yugoslavia, which is expected to arrive about November 20.

subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext: What about their medical examinations?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext: The immigration team will take care of that aspect of the situation, but this is essentially a humanitarian refugee movement.

subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext: Does the minister intend to reverse the previous policy of admitting even those who could not satisfy the medical requirements, if they were otherwise satisfactory?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know that I can give a categorical answer to the question in the form in which it was asked. I think we would have to look at every case and see just what were the implications. That is one of the purposes of sending the team; but as the house knows, because of the emergency and humanitarian nature of this movement, it is a fact that standards of admissibility were relaxed. The humanitarian aspects of the situation are accentuated here because if somebody does not take these refugees they will be in a really desperate position during this winter in Yugoslavia.

subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext: I should like to ask another supplementary question, if I may, Mr. Speaker. Will the minister consider very carefully continuing the policy of receiving a fair proportion of those who cannot satisfy the medical requirements, instead of leaving them on the doorstep of another country? That was the policy we have followed up to now, and I think we should continue it.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext: Since it was put in the form of a question I can assure the hon. member and the house that the fullest and most sympathetic consideration will be given to the principle that he has put forward, but I cannot give a categorical answer as to just what are the details of the standards that will be applied to each case.

subtopic: ACCEPTANCE OF GROUP FROM YUGOSLAVIA
speechtext:
I have a related question to ask the minister. I would like the minister, if he could, to tell the house whether we are continuing to take Hungarian refugees from Austria. I believe there are some 30,000 in that country.
Inquiries of the Ministry

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. Would the Prime Minister care to comment on the report that Canada's Minister of Agriculture at the FAO conference in Rome has expressed opposition to the proposal that the FAO budget be increased by $2 million?
In view of the critical world food problem, both in deficit and surplus areas, does the Prime Minister not feel that such a modest increase for FAO purposes is justified?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORTED CANADIAN OPPOSITION TO INCREASED BUDGET

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman was kind enough to forward to me a copy of the press dispatch to which he has made reference. My own attitude, and I am sure that of the minister, is that FAO has done an outstanding job in correlating the activities of agriculture in all parts of the world represented in that organization. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: CODFISH-STATEMENT ON REPORTED ACTION BY JAMAICA TO SHUT OUT IMPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was asked a question yesterday by the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick) in these terms:
Will the minister state what action the government is taking in connection with the threatened

action of the government of Jamaica in shutting out the imports of salt codfish from the Atlantic provinces?
Acting on instructions, the Canadian trade commissioner in Jamaica has had interviews with both the chief minister and the minister of trade and industry in Jamaica, at which time a full explanation of our desire to continue to trade on a friendly and unrestricted basis was placed before the Jamaican officials. The reasons why increased prices were needed for salt codfish were fully explained. The Jamaican officials were informed that Canadian fishermen would suffer if a satisfactory settlement was not reached, and that it was hoped that the threat to prohibit imports from Canada would be removed.
In reply the Jamaican chief minister denied that imports of Canadian salt codfish are to be prohibited. He further stated that the government of Jamaica planned to invite tenders from all sources of supply for its requirements of 4,800 metric tons. The closing date for tenders is today, November 8. Consequently, the Canadian salt fish trade have submitted tenders through our trade commissioner in Jamaica, and we are awaiting the result.

speechtext:
On November 1 the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) asked me this question:
Can the minister tell the house whether the government of the province of Quebec has made an application to his department under the Navigable Waters Protection Act for the development of power in the Lachine section of the St. Lawrence river?

The answer to that supplementary question is yes. In 1956 the Quebec Hydro Electric Commission asked what technical demands or requirements would be imposed on the commission by the Department of Public Works in connection with the Lachine water power project. The reply was made that the interests of the Department of Public Works would appear to be limited to the protection of navigation, but other departments would also be concerned. Nothing further transpired between the Department of Public Works and the Quebec Hydro Electric Commission.

Pension Act PENSION ACT

The house resumed, from Wednesday, November 6, consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Brooks-Mr. Courtemanche in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Pension Act to place dependants of persons who served in world war II in a position comparable to that of dependants of persons who served in world war I in cases of disability or death due to improper conduct; to ensure that pensions may be paid to the dependants of deceased members of the forces resident and domiciled in Newfoundland; to provide for the continuation of disability pensions and widows' pensions to the end of the month in which death occurred except in cases where no additional pension for dependants is payable; to provide for the payment of pension to the daughter of a pensioned widower where the domestic establishment is maintained after his death; to provide for an increase in the clothing allowance on account of amputation or use of appliances; to provide for an increase in the allowances for funeral and burial expenses; to remove the limitation on the amount of pension payable to a dependent parent of a deceased pensioner after discontinuance of pension to other dependants; to authorize payment of widows' pensions at current rates upon reinstatement of discontinued pension; and to remove the limitation on payment of pensions to or in respect of children born after a specified date, or to wives whose marriage to a member of the forces or a pensioner took place after a specified date; such measure to include, in addition, certain consequential and clarifying amendments.
Is the minister not going to make a statement?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to make a statement. This resolution is somewhat extensive, because it lists the majority of the features in the amending bill. Many of these have been designed to clarify sections of the act in which some doubt regarding interpretation has existed. My intention is to outline the main features and, after listening to the remarks of hon. members, to give more detailed information and costs on second reading and when the bill is in committee.
The purpose of the bill is to provide, in general, for additional benefits for former members of the forces and their dependants, and to bring other benefits more in line with the increases in the basic scale of pensions for disability and death which became effective last July. I should like now to quote from the resolution.
... to provide for the continuation of disability pensions and widows' pensions to the end of the month in which death occurred except in cases where no additional pension for dependants is payable . . .
The act at the present time provides that an award of disability pension shall cease

on the date of death, and it then becomes the responsibility of the commission to determine whether death was attributable to service.
1.	The dependants are pensionable when death was attributable to service irrespective of the rate at which pension was in payment at the date of death.
2.	The widow and children are pensionable when pension was in payment at 50 per cent or more at the date of death.
The amendment, as it stated in the resolution, provides for the continuation of pension to the end of the month in which death occurred provided additional pension was in payment for the dependants. In a number of cases, death has no service relationship, and the effect of this amendment will be to permit the continuation of the pension income to the home at a time when there is great distress and, in a number of instances, need.
I quote another clause of the resolution: . . . to provide for an increase in the clothing allowance on account of amputation or use of appliances. . . .
The act at the present time makes the following provision for wear and tear of clothing:
1.	For leg amputation cases, $72 per year.
2.	For arm amputation cases, $30 per year.
3.	For other pension cases wherein the wearing of an appliance causes excessive wear and tear of clothing, not exceeding $72.
These rates have been in effect for some years and the intention is to increase them.
A further clause in the resolution reads:
To provide for an increase in the allowances for funeral and burial expenses . . .
The act gives the commission discretion to pay an amount not exceeding $185 when a disability pensioner dies and his estate is not sufficient to pay the expenses of his last sickness and burial. This total is made up of the following maximum payments:
1.	$110 in respect of funeral services.
2.	$25 for cemetery charges.
3.	$50 for the expenses of the pensioner's last sickness.
Those are the present rates, Mr. Chairman. The intention is to provide for an increase in these allowances in order that they may be more closely related to those paid by the department and to present day conditions.
I quote further from the resolution:
. . . to remove the limitation on payment of pensions to or in respect of children born after a specified date, or to wives whose marriage to a member of the forces or a pensioner took place after a specified date . . .
This, I may say, is to do away with the world war I date line or deadline, as it is sometimes called. The act provides in the

case of a world war I disability pensioner that no additional pension shall be paid when marriage or remarriage takes place on or after the 1st day of May, 1954. This restrictive measure was first introduced on May 1, 1933. It was subsequently advanced to the 1st of May of the following years, 1944, 1948, 1951, and now stands at May 1, 1954. The restriction in the statute applies to world war I pensioners and not to world war II pensioners. There is no date line as far as world war II pensioners are concerned.
The intention is, as intimated in the resolution, to remove the time limitation. There is provision in the Pension Act against so-called death-bed marriages which gives the commission discretion where the death of the husband has occurred less than one year subsequent to the date of marriage.
Provision is made in the bill for the amendments to the Pension Act which became effective on July 1, 1957, by authority of Appropriation Act No. 4, 1957. This was under Bill No. 418, to which we referred previously, and item 670 of the supplementary estimates at that time. This is part of the tidying up process, incorporating into the Pension Act payments which are being made as from July 1.
The other amendments, as I stated earlier, are mainly clarifying and do not infringe on any existing benefits, nor do they incur any added liability. I will be very pleased to give further information on second reading and when the clauses of the bill are before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, at the present time I wish to deal more with what the resolution does not do than what it does do. What it proposes to do is the sort of thing to meet difficulties that have arisen in the administration of the act and remove apparent inequities in cases affecting small groups who are benefiting from the Pension Act, or should benefit. It is the sort of thing that has to be done from time to time with respect to a statute like the Pension Act. Some of the provisions have to do with such things as increasing the clothing allowance in the case of a person drawing a pension in respect of an amputation, and are related to the rising cost of living.
These provisions are important, but they do not affect the general body of pensioners. However, to the extent that they meet certain needs of the various groups with which they deal, in accordance with the past attitude of the party with which I am associated these measures will receive very strong approval.
As I see it, the difficulty about the resolution is that in dealing with basic rates of pension
Pension Act
it only goes so far as to confirm what was done by the last government before the election, and it does not propose to increase the basic rates at all. In view of the strong attitude taken at that time by the members of the present government when in opposition in finding fault with the increases in basic rates brought into effect by the then government, I think people generally expected that the basic rates would be dealt with.
Hon. members will recall that at that time fault was found because it was said that the raising of the basic rates was an urgent matter and the government had not gone far enough, and the promise was held out that if the Progressive Conservative party was elected this matter would be dealt with at once. The cost of living has been rising steadily since then. If the matter was as urgent as was represented by the present members of the government, who were then in opposition, it is difficult to understand why the government has not dealt with this matter. The government has continually held out the idea that it is proceeding to carry out the promises on which it was elected.
There has been some suggestion that there is going to be a sudden election. However, even if things go as well, and along the lines indicated by the present Minister of Veterans Affairs, and there is a session after Christmas at which the matter is considered by the veterans affairs committee, the earliest date on which these pensioners can receive the benefit of any increase, which government supporters said this spring was so important, will be one year from that date. In other words it will be the following spring. I am sure this will come as a surprise to the veteran and a surprise to the whole country, especially in the light of what was said by the present Prime Minister during the last election campaign. For example, in a telecast on May 22, 1957, the present Prime Minister dealt with this matter. I shall quote from what he said:
We believe the old age pension is inadequate. We intend, this September, to call together parliament, and there and then fix a fair and reasonable amount for the old age pensioner,-
Then he goes on to say:
-indeed for the other pensioners, and also make provision for a formula whereby due allowance will be made in the future for the rising cost of living, providing that it continues.
If ever a person could make a definite pledge, Mr. Chairman, it would be when he carefully considered what he was going to say in a telecast to the nation. The statement is in such definite terms-"indeed, for other pensioners". What was going to be done for other pensions?

Pension Act

May I point out to the hon. member that he was speaking of old age security and other pensioners, blind pensioners, disabled persons. The pension has been raised from $46 to $55, and the bill is already through the house.

I would point out to the
minister that the Prime Minister, speaking on behalf of the Conservative party, mentioned the old age pensioners, and indeed other persons. Now then, other pensioners, outside of old age pensioners, would be blind pensioners. Would my hon. friend suggest that when the present leader of his party was speaking of other pensioners he was referring only to the small group of blind pensioners, and that his remarks had no reference to the great group of ex-service pensioners? Surely the ex-servicemen are an important body of pensioners.

That is going to be given
careful study.

My friend says that is going
to be given consideration.
Careful study.
Only careful study?
Study and consideration.

We were promised more than study. Let me read again to hon. members what was stated. Why are these promises being whittled down to cover only blind pensioners when the Prime Minister said "... indeed, for other pensioners"? Are not ex-servicemen other pensioners? Here is what the leader of the Conservative party said:
We intend, this September-
A session was not called in September because of Her Majesty's visit. We now have a session called, and it was called as soon as possible to carry out the promises.
-and there and then-
No doubt about that.
-fix a fair and reasonable amount for the old age pensioners, indeed for the other pensioners.
Does the minister say that, here and now, they are fixing what they consider to be a fair and reasonable amount for the service pensioners? Then let me read to the minister what his leader said to the nation concerning another matter which was to be considered at the session this fall. There was going to be action, and here is what his leader said:
.	.	. and also make provision for a formula
whereby due allowance will be made in the future for the rising cost of living, providing that it continues.
Everyone knows the cost of living is continuing to rise. Figures put on the record

by various hon. members, and indeed by the Minister of National Health and Welfare on November 4, showed that the consumer price index has continued to rise. On the basis of 1949 being equal to 100 the index had risen in 1955 to 116.4, and now stands at 122.6. If this matter was so urgent this spring it is even more urgent now. The minister's leader said that, there and then-he meant at a session in September-he was going to make provision for a formula whereby due allowance will be made in the future for the rising cost of living, provided it continued. There is a definite pledge to the people. I think the present Prime Minister, who was then leader of the opposition-

I should like to ask the hon. member a question. Did his government take into consideration the rising cost of living when they increased the pension as of July 1? If they did, it has not been very long from July 1 to date.

The point with which I am dealing is that the increases which were brought into effect at that time were denounced by hon. members opposite. It was in the light of these increases that the Prime Minister made this telecast. In other words, these increases had already been brought forward, and it was in the light of these increases which were denounced by the present members of the government as inadequate that their leader made this speech.

I think, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is implying that the increases were not sufficient. What representation did he make to his government before July 1 as to the insufficiency of the amounts? Did he make any? I doubt very much that he did.
I am not debating the action that was taken at the spring session of parliament, because what was done then was placed before the people.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It sure was.

Hon. members opposite are gloating over the results of that election. They held out certain promises to the people, and all I am saying is this, that people who gloat over being elected as a result of these promises should be the first to stand up and say "Now, let us fulfil the promises on which we did get elected".
Seme hon. Members: Hear, hear.

The attitude of their leader was very definite on this matter. For example, he is reported as having said this at Victoria on May 22, 1957, at about the time of this other telecast. He is reported as saying "We

Pension Act
will provide fair and realistic pensions based on the cost of living and a fair comfort in living". Then he went on to say this:
I say our promise will be carried out. That is my idea of public life. Promises must bear a distinct mark of responsibility.
Here was their leader not only holding out these promises but saying:
I say our promise will be carried out. That is my idea of public life.
We have made a good start on them.
My hon. friend is saying they have made a good start.
In a few months, we have done more than you did in 22 years in some of them.
But his leader said, "I do not believe in making irresponsible promises; what I promise will be carried out".
That is what we are on now.

What was his promise? His promise was that at the session in September, there and then, pensions would be increased and they would be tied to the cost of living or a formula would be established "whereby due allowance will be made in future for the rising cost of living providing that it continues". I wonder whether my hon. friends opposite, in their minds, really believe that a promise to study this matter and perhaps do something about it a year later is carrying out a promise that within a matter of four months this matter would be dealt with in a certain definite way, namely by increases with provision for a formula in the acts tying the pension to the cost of living.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, may I say this. The hon. member has taken a sentence out of context. As I remember it, the Prime Minister was speaking of old age security at that time, and he said that old age pensions and other pensions which he had been mentioning would be dealt with at this session. They have been dealt with.
Oh, no; they have not been dealt with. The promises have not been carried out.
Mr. Chairman, I am only dealing with this matter as I read it.
You are taking one sentence out of a whole context.

No. When the Prime Minister said, as I read to the house, that this September he would deal with old age pensions and indeed with other pensions, is my hon. friend
suggesting that people listening to that speech would know that he did not mean veterans
pensions?
Having heard his previous remarks, yes. You have taken only one sentence out of the whole context.

I have read the whole thing having to do with what the present Prime Minister said. He said this, and I take it that he said it deliberately. He spoke first of the old age pensioner, and he said, "indeed for the other pensioners". Is my hon. friend trying to tell us now that his leader intended to say that they were going to increase old age pensions and were going to tie them to the cost of living, but that he had no intention of doing anything like that for service pensioners, or in other words that he did not intend to do as much for service pensioners as he was doing for others?

The Prime Minister realized that there could be a review of the Pension Act. Such a review of the Pension Act takes a considerable time. It is with regard to the veterans pensions. As I stated in this house, Mr. Chairman, it is the intention to review the Pension Act at the next session.
That is not what you said before June 10.

That is, of course, exactly what I have been trying to say, namely that his leader held out one promise to the people and that now it is not being carried out in this legislation. If the minister admits that they are not keeping this important promise, I am satisfied. Surely the keeping of a promise to increase the basic rates and to tie them to the cost of living this fall was much more important than clearing up the small points, important as they are, which are dealt with in this legislation. Surely the raising of the basic rates affecting all pensioners, which rates were held out by hon. members opposite when they were in opposition as being so inadequate, was an important matter. As to the promise they made that they were going to be dealt with this fall, surely if they were going to deal with them at all they should have dealt with the main point of attack they made on the government last spring and during the election campaign.
Your government considered them adequate to July 1, or just a few months ago.

Mr. Chairman, I believe in democracy as, I think, do most of us here. When our government set the amount which they indicated was as far as they were ready

Pension Act
to go at that particular time, the hon. member's leader and his associates said, "We think something should be done this fall to go much further", and the people indicated their approval. Now I am just asking them to do what they promised to do, on the basis of which they are sitting where they are today. That is all I am doing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The people also indicated disapproval of you.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member whether he would not agree that if everyone in this house had the opportunity to speak, and spoke as long as has the hon. member, we would not get even the emergency legislation through at this time.
More closure.

I do not intend to deal with the point of order, Mr. Chairman, because I do not think it can be said the opposition have unduly held up the war veterans allowance bill. On the first day it was introduced it went through all stages, or rather it went through second reading, the committee stage and, by consent, third reading. I wonder whether it is fair to make a statement such as the one which has just been made, in view of the fact that there is that co-operation shown not only by the party with which I am associated but by all parties in this house to forward this legislation. Is my hon. friend suggesting that when his government speaks nobody else dare say anything, that they must just say "Aye"?
No, no.
He can speak on the whole problem, as suggested by the hon. member.

After listening to his leader indicate his disapproval of that idea, suggesting that members should be heard from and that whatever the government said should not be accepted without comment, I think such a suggestion should come from any place else in the whole house but from the place whence it came, right behind his leader.
What a transformation.
I agree with that statement. It is indeed a transformation.
On your part.

It is indeed a transformation, having heard day after day about the fact that hon. members were not saying enough, that the government was having its way without the members being heard from enough. Then when a spokesman for the official opposition is pointing out that it would

be a good thing for the government to carry out its promises, a man on the opposition side of the house rises and objects to 40 minutes being taken to deal with this most important matter. Verily it is a real transformation.
You are not suffering from closure at the present time.

Of course, Mr. Chairman, I am not surprised that hon. members opposite, faced with this situation wherein there is an open breach of a promise they made to the veterans of this country, should be raising all these spurious points of order and trying to divert me from presenting that viewpoint. I don't blame them, but it just shows how uneasy they are in their own consciences about the thing they are bringing forward.
Mr. Chairman, when the suggestion of increasing these pensions was brought in by the last government, it was dealt with as an emergency measure because it was thought that there should be an election, and rather than have the pensioners wait for an increase until after that was over, an increase was given. That was an emergency, because in order to have an election in June, as was asked for by all parties-the present government party was as anxious to have an election as anybody else-it was necessary to dissolve parliament in April, and accordingly the increase had to be granted before that date. But despite these circumstances there were demands that the matter should go before a committee. Surely there is more time now in which to deal with this question than there was last spring.
Then again there were demands and statements that the amount should be raised because it was not enough. I do not think it can be denied that the present leader of the house and Minister of Public Works was one of the outstanding and acknowledged spokesmen for his party on veterans affairs. His position was such that he was recognized as one of the real spokesmen of the Progressive Conservative party on this matter. What did he say with regard to the announced intention by the government of that time, as an emergency measure, to tide over the veterans until this matter could be dealt with in the ordinary way by a veterans affairs committee? I am satisfied, Mr. Chairman-
Then sit down.
What did you say?

I understand. You don't like the quotations. You don't like to hear quotations from your present leaders showing what they said while in opposition. If it was something said before the election that would gather votes, you were ready to cheer. Now, when it is a matter of delivering the goods, you don't want to hear them.
You don't want us to deliver the goods.

That is what I am asking you to do. The bill deals with relatively small, though important, matters, and the main thing you said you were going to deal with you say you are going to let stand till next year-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

Mr. Chairman, before making a few remarks on the subject matter of the resolution now before us, I should like to say that the C.C.F. group was originally to have been led on this important question by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, but he is away today attending the NATO conference. I have been asked to substitute for him, and I do so with pleasure.
We are grateful that the government has indicated in resolution No. 9 that some of the problems which arise in connection with the Pension Act will be dealt with very shortly, but I think it must be a matter of keen disappointment to hon. members and to all veterans that no provision is being made in this resolution for an increase in the basic rate of disability pension. I do not propose to take seriously what has been said on the subject by the hon. member for Rosthern-
Nobody does.

It
is very hard to take seriously his complaints on that subject when for so long his government failed to bring these disability rates up even to the level of those paid for common and unskilled labour. And that should be the test under this act.
This act gives veterans, as a right, not as a matter of charity or social assistance, an amount which is supposed to put them in as good a position as if they had not suffered their war disabilities. Unfortunately, the rate of pensions has gradually lagged behind the

Pension Act
cost of living on one hand and the rate for even common labour at union rates on the other; it has lagged behind the increase in our gross national product, and again I say it is a matter for keen disappointment that this government has not seen fit to go further at this time than the Liberal government did on March 14 of last year.
In the short time that has elapsed since March 14, 1956, the cost of living in Canada has increased by approximately 4 per cent. This means, for instance, that the rate of $200 a month for a totally disabled married veteran since that time has already suffered a shrinkage of $8. In the light of what has been said previously by prominent members of the Conservative party, and in the light of their attacks on the inadequacy of the increase of March 14, 1956, which became effective in July, I do not think they are justified in failing to bring in further increases at this time.
The proposal of the Canadian Legion that the increases instituted in March, 1956, should have been 33-J per cent and not an average of 17 per cent, which was as far as the government of that day was prepared to go, represents a modest request. As a matter of fact it strikes me that the veterans of Canada have a most honourable and enviable record in the matter of the requests they have made to governments of Canada for adjustments in pension rates. They have not made the excessive demands which I think have been made in some other countries; instead, they have merely asked that the disabled veteran be placed in the position where he has not actually suffered loss as a result of his war service and, of course, monetary pensions must fall far short of that. In view of the rise in the cost of living since the Legion first requested a 33J per cent increase their present request in my opinion is a very modest one.
We are opening up the Pension Act by means of this resolution for many rather detailed and complicated changes. It seems to me, therefore, this is clearly a case where a standing committee on veterans affairs should have been appointed, or at least a special committee should have been called together to consider the bill the minister Will present to the house. We do not want to delay the passage of any legislation designed to improve the Pension Act, but we have been sitting in this session of parliament since October 14, which would have provided ample time for a special committee to be called together to consider this legislation. I am convinced that the representatives of the veterans organizations would be pleased to come to Ottawa quickly and
[Mr. Macdonald (Vancouver-Kingsway) .1
present their views, and I believe the committee could be called together, perform its function and report back to the house within a period of two weeks. In view of the ambiguities which do undoubtedly still exist in the Pension Act it is a pity the government has not yet proposed that this procedure be followed.
I would now like to refer to what was said by the present house leader on July 11, 1956, as reported at page 5867 of Hansard of that date. The hon. member informed the house in extremely definite terms;
When we form a government, we certainly will have a full-time Minister of Veterans Affairs and we certainly will have a standing committee on veterans affairs.
Unfortunately there are many wrinkles in the Pension Act that are not going to be ironed out by the measures indicated in this resolution, and when you try to deal with an act as complicated as this on a piecemeal basis without it being referred to a committee for thorough study, you are bound to leave many injustices in the wording of the act.
I would like to briefly refer to some of the good things in the resolution before us. Of course we are all pleased that the veteran of world war I who did not embark on the sea of matrimony until after May 1, 1954, is finally going to get some recognition for his wife. It is surely a praiseworthy matter that such a veteran did not. reach a decision to marry too quickly, that some have given long and careful consideration to this important step. However, the resolution does not propose that any recognition will be accorded to the children of such veterans. Are we to assume that a veteran of world war I who did not marry until after May 1, 1954, cannot have children? I think we would be making a big mistake if we decided this, because this philosophy has been contradicted many times already in this country. I would ask that this part of the resolution be extended so the families of such veterans may be protected.
Another matter not dealt with in the resolution is the status of the common law wife of a veteran. Under the Pension Act the common law wife of a veteran is recognized if they lived together as man and wife at the time of enlistment and she had then been publicly known as his wife. Unfortunately there are many cases of veterans who, finding themselves unable to marry, live in a common law union after their service to their country has been rendered, and their wives are not recognized as having official status under the act. It is unfortunate that in legislation in the parliament of Canada we

should have to consider giving recognition to the position of common law wives, but as long as we have medieval divorce laws in this country, as long as divorce cannot be obtained even on the grounds of incurable insanity, in the case of a wife deserted without means by her husband or even on the ground of cruelty resulting in a breakdown of health, we must realize that common law liaisons are bound to take place. Many children have been born to common law unions and have grown up to become good citizens. It seems to me this resolution should go further and accord recognition to the common law wife of a veteran who has lived with him and perhaps done a fine job in raising a family but, due to the archaic divorce laws prevailing in Canada, the couple have not been able to have the union regularized.
There is another case I think should be dealt with, and I hope the government will consider including a clause in the bill when it is introduced in this house to cover the situation. That is the case of a British subject who joined the British forces in world war I and who was not at that time a Canadian. He might have been living in England and joined the British forces but since world war I has been living in this country, has become a Canadian citizen and been domiciled here. Such a veteran may receive a modest pension from the British government but he is not recognized at all under our Pension Act; the supplementary sections of that act, Nos. 50 to 53, do not help that particular individual. Surely he is a deserving case. There are many veterans who joined the forces of the British commonwealth, probably in England, before or at the time of the outbreak of world war I and who at the present time are in receipt of pensions from the British government of not more than $4, $6 or $8 a month.
I am particularly pleased to see that the government in this resolution proposes an increase in the clothing allowance for amputation cases and I suppose that allowance would also be increased for paraplegics, but I am afraid it does not fully cover the needs of this particular class of veteran. A married paraplegic veteran is considered totally disabled.
He would receive $200 a month and in addition $120 a month helplessness allowance. But I respectfully suggest to the government, Mr. Chairman, that this is not adequate. In addition to the wheel chair, of course, these people need special housing; they need ramps in their houses; they need larger doors. They
Pension Act
cannot move into houses that have too small rooms and they require transportation by automobile, perhaps with special equipment in it, not as a luxury, as is the case with other people, but as a matter of necessity.
Therefore I would hope the government, through the minister, when they introduce the bill will give further consideration to increasing the helplessness allowance of the paraplegic cases. I understand that at the present time-and I hope I am wrong-these cases do not receive the full helplessness allowance unless the veteran is completely and at all times bedridden. Perhaps when the minister makes his statement he will clarify that point because, if it is the case, I think it is a most unjust situation.
Another point I think should be dealt with when the government brings in the bill is the vexed question, which has been raised many times by members now sitting on the government side, of diseases or injuries of pre-enlistment origin. Many claims are rejected, of course, by the pension commission at the present time because they rule that the disease or injury was of pre-enlistment origin. Yet the man will have had his medical examination when he enlisted in the forces, and that disease or injury would not appear on the medical report. We say that in such a case there should be a presumption, if the injury or disease does not show up on the medical examination, that it was not of pre-enlistment origin.
The house leader, then the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra dealt with this question in 1956, at page 5868 of Hansard, in these words:
I believe the time has come to write into that act a presumption that injury or disease occurred after enlistment.
I could go further into the quotation, but this indicates his thinking at that time. This is an additional reason why a committee, even a special committee, of this house is badly needed, so that in addition to the improvements in the legislation which the government is indicating in the resolution, other improvements can be made to make this a model piece of legislation for the disabled veteran.
I should like to close, Mr. Chairman, with one final point. I regret that the resolution does not deal with the retroactivity of the pension awards. When an applicant applies to the pension commission he may find that to establish his claim takes as much as two years. It may take longer before he has got together the witnesses and the evidence he needs to establish his claim; but once granted by the pension commission that pension should date back to the date of application of the

Pension Act
veteran. Again I say that in the Pension Act we are not dealing with any kind oi social assistance; we are dealing with something that belongs as of right to the veteran, and if the commission rules finally that the veteran was entitled to the pension on his application, then it should be made retroactive to the date of the application.
Certainly that is the rule if a company goes through the courts, perhaps up to the exchequer court, with a claim that it is entitled to, say, special depreciation on its equipment to write off against taxable income. If, after years of litigation, the court rules that the company was correct in its contention of course it dates back automatically without question to the date of the application. When we do that with financial matters and with company matters we should see that the veterans pension dates back to the date of application. There could very well be in the act a saving provision to the effect that this would not revive old claims existing, say, prior to the last war. I do not suggest that that should be done, but with such a saving provision surely pensions could be made retroactive.
I have finished with the proposals that I hope the government will take into consideration, Mr. Chairman, but in conclusion I want to say my main point is that I regret the government has not increased the basic rate in its disability pensions. Frankly, I do not think we are living up to the standards with our veterans that we do in the financial and material sense. When war equipment or material is damaged or destroyed we replace it at once without question. The companies which produced war materials in the last war received not only profits but often write-offs on their capital costs, so that in effect they got a gift of the capital equipment they were using during the war. The biggest case in point, of course, was the special write-off allowed to the Aluminum Company of Canada for its work at Arvida, which resulted in effect in that company being given a gift of that huge power installation.
We have to ask ourselves whether we are treating the veteran on the human level as well as we are treating the financial aspects of fighting a war. In view of that it does not seem to me that these pension rates at the present time do put the veteran in the position where it can be said that he has not suffered loss as a result of incurring injury or disease in the service of his country. To the extent that we can remedy that situation by financial measures we should generously and quickly do so.

It is one o'clock. I wish to go on this afternoon, but I understand the Minister of Trade and Commerce has an important announcement to make at 2.30 o'clock. Might I ask that we rise and report progress?
Progress reported.
At one o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: COMPOSITION AND MATTERS TO BE DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether I might have the opportunity now, which I asked for this morning, to make an announcement to the house with regard to the trade mission which is going to proceed to the United Kingdom. I presume I may do so under leave to revert to motions.
The Canadian trade mission to the United Kingdom, comprising leading representatives of business and industry from all areas of Canada, will leave Montreal for London on Thursday, November 21. The mission will also include representatives of labour, agriculture and fisheries. The purpose of the mission is to stimulate purchases from United Kingdom sources of goods now imported by Canada from non-commonwealth countries. Its immediate objectives are to provide a favourable climate and to seek specific opportunities for the expansion of British exports to Canada, so that Canada may take full advantage of sources of supply in the United Kingdom, and British exporters may participate increasingly in Canada's growing import requirements.
To this end, membership of the mission consists largely of businessmen whose companies represent some 20 groups of industries across Canada which, it is believed, can use increasing quantities of British products. The mission represents an annual purchasing potential of many millions of dollars worth of imports.
The mission will depart from Dorval airport, Montreal, on the late afternoon of November 21 and will arrive in London the next morning. It will remain in the United Kingdom from November 22 until December 18, during which time it will follow a program arranged by the United Kingdom authorities in consultation with Canada House.

Following preliminary talks in London with ministers, senior government officials, the dollar export council and its affiliated industrial bodies, visits will be made to important centres of industry and commerce throughout Great Britain to permit of direct factory and plant visits and meetings with British exporters and businessmen. The mission will conclude its visit with final conferences to be held in London from December 16 to 18.
The list of names of those who have accepted an invitation to join the mission will be released today. The list is complete except for the addition of two representatives of agriculture from whom I am awaiting word and except for one or two changes which will result from withdrawals that are expected because of personal reasons on the part of those who have already accepted an invitation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: COMPOSITION AND MATTERS TO BE DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure all members of the house will welcome the statement made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) and do and will extend their very best wishes to him and to those who will be accompanying him on this mission. There is no doubt that greater diversification of our import trade would be beneficial to our economy, and the government has come to the concluson that this is apt to be an effective way of furthering that objective. We hope that their prognostics or hopes in that regard will be realized and that there will be the furthering of what has been, I think, the desire and objective of all parties in the house, to see restored to the greatest possible extent the multilateral trade that used to exist and that did have beneficial effects for all those who could participate in that mutual trade.
There have been dislocations which brought about inevitable results. I hope those results are not to be permanently inevitable and that they can be overcome. I can assure the minister that we wish him well in his endeavours to restore as near an approach to multilateral trade as can be realized under present world conditions.

subtopic: COMPOSITION AND MATTERS TO BE DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we join very heartily, of course, with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. St. Laurent) in wishing this delegation every success in Great Britain. I noted that in the minister's statement-I understand why, of course-he laid particular stress on the desirability of British exports to Canada. I am sure that the delegation will not lose sight of
Trade Mission to United Kingdom the other side in which we are also very interested, namely the question of enlarging our exports to the United Kingdom. The more imports we take from the United Kingdom and commonwealth countries, the more we provide them with the necessary dollars which they can spend in Canada for the exports that we wish to send abroad.
Representing, as I do, an agricultural constituency, a wheat-growing area, I am anxious to see an expansion of trade with the United Kingdom not only for industry generally but particularly to help our agricultural situation. Even if the list of gentlemen who are going to England has not been completed, if the minister has the list there I would ask him if he would like to table a partial list this afternoon and add to it later.

subtopic: COMPOSITION AND MATTERS TO BE DISCUSSED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to join the other two speakers in wishing the minister every success. I hope the result can be a substantial expansion of trade with Great Britain and the sterling area generally. I should like to ask the minister this question. In view of the success of the United States surplus disposal program in making surplus food available to nations that are not able to obtain it through the normal channels of trade, while at the same time substantially increasing their sales for dollars, will the minister give consideration to the advisability of Canada accepting sterling under a firm agreement that such sterling will be spent within the sterling area so that it may be used to buy goods which we are at present buying from the United States, thereby helping to reduce our imbalance of trade with the United States and at the same time helping Britain to reduce her imbalance of trade with Canada?
