speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure we all agree with previous speakers that anything that can be done to advance trade relations and increase trade is very commendable, but I should like to ask the minister a question, if I may.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: COMPOSITION AND MATTERS TO BE DISCUSSED
speechtext:
Order. As I understand the practice when statements of this kind are made, and I am sure the house will correct me if I am in error, it has been customary for a spokesman for each party to be given the opportunity to comment on the statement but it is not customary to ask questions or to open the door beyond that. I think we would do well to confine ourselves to the practice of having one comment from each group in the house, which we have now had. I would ask my hon. friend to defer his question until the next period when such questions are dealt with.

Pension Act PENSION ACT

The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Brooks -Mr. Courtemanche in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Pension Act to place dependants of persons who served in world war II in a position comparable to that of dependants of persons who served in world war I in cases of disability or death due to improper conduct; to ensure that pensions may he paid to the dependants of deceased members of the forces resident and domiciled in Newfoundland; to provide for the continuation of disability pensions and widows' pensions to the end of the month in which death occurred except in cases where no additional pension for dependants is payable; to provide for the payment of pension to the daughter of a pensioned widower where the domestic establishment is maintained after his death; to provide for an increase in the clothing allowance on account of amputation or use of appliances; to provide for an increase in the allowances for funeral and burial expenses; to remove the limitation on the amount of pension payable to a dependent parent of a deceased pensioner after discontinuance of pension to other dependants; to authorize payment of widows' pensions at current rates upon reinstatement of discontinued pensions; and to remove the limitation on payment of pensions to or in respect of children born after a specified date, or to wives whose marriage to a member of the forces or a pensioner took place after a specified date; such measure to include, in addition, certain consequential and clarifying amendments.

Mr. Chairman, before the resumption of the debate on the resolution I should like to make an observation regarding a remark by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway. I did not wish to interrupt him at the time he was speaking. He expressed his pleasure regarding the removal of the dateline for the marriage or remarriage of world war I veterans and mentioned his disappointment because the resolution did not say anything about children. Naturally the resolution is abbreviated, and I am happy to assure the hon. member and other members of the committee that the bill which will be introduced provides for the removal of the dateline with respect to marriage and also to children.
am glad to have that assurance, Mr. Chairman.

I listened with some degree
of disfavour to the hon. member for Rosthern as he made his contribution to this debate. It seemed to me his speech had nothing to do with the resolution and contributed nothing to either the welfare of the veterans or the subject matter under discussion. I doubt very much that the veterans will thank him for his remarks or that his constituents will approve of his attitude. On the other hand, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway was extremely instructive and I hope, sir, I can do as well as he did.

At this point, Mr. Chairman, I want to pay tribute to those responsible for the administration of veterans' affairs in British Columbia. So far as that province, at least, is concerned, they have been extremely efficient and extremely careful to interpret the regulations and the act under their administration as well as they possibly could. I should like to pay particular tribute to General Roaf, while he was the administrator for British Columbia.
In so far as these proposals are concerned, an assessment of the extent of them indicates the obvious necessity for a permanent committee on veterans affairs. No legislation as important as this should be permitted to get into such a state of desuetude as the proposals in this resolution would indicate. I express regret on behalf of the veterans of Canada that no provision is made in this bill for a rise in the basic pension. I know, Mr. Chairman, that Rome was not built in a day. I know that this government cannot do everything all at once, but at the same time they could have gone a long way towards helping the veterans of this country by raising the basic pension to a point where it would be at least equal to the salaries and wages received by the lower classes of labour in this country.
I should like to quote from page 5 of the veterans brief which was presented the day before yesterday to the cabinet. On that page it will be noted that in 1920 a single pensioner received $900 and today under this measure he will be receiving $1,800; that is a rise of 100 per cent. The same situation applies to a married pensioner. His pension goes from $1,200 in 1920 to $2,400 in 1957. The widow is not so fortunate because she was receiving $720 in 1920 and is now to receive $1,380, a rise of $660. When we compare these pensions with the pay of the armed forces and with that of some members of the civil service, we find a great difference. We find that a single private-please remember that this is the initial payment, and do not forget that a private can rise through the various grades of private and receive a considerably increased emolument -in 1920 was receiving $930.75, and today is receiving $1,980. A married private in the army was receiving $1,130.75 in 1920, and today he is getting $2,700, that is a rise of $1,569. When we come to the civil service, we find something else. A customs guard in 1920 was getting $1,260 and today he is getting $3,360. A cleaner and helper in 1920 was getting $900, the same as a pensioner on that date, and today he is getting $2,910.
Now, may we examine this in the light of the brief that was presented last year, Mr. Chairman. I should like to point out to you

that the condition of the pensioner, as compared with these categories, has deteriorated even in the one year. The brief last year was presented on November 9, and let us have a look at it. On a percentage basis the pension of a single pensioner had risen 66 per cent on that date and the pension has now risen 100 per cent. The pension for a married pensioner has risen approximately the same amount and the same is true of a widow's pension. However, when we come to examine the others, we find that the single private in the army has received pay increases amounting to nearly 108 per cent in 1956, and 112.7 per cent in 1957. The married private had received pay increases amounting to 134.4 per cent in 1956 and is now up over 154 per cent. The customs guard received pay increases amounting to 166 per cent between 1920 and 1957. I should like to point out to you that in 1956 his percentage rise in pay was then 154 per cent, and it went up again this year. The pension has not gone up that much.
In the light of these figures, Mr. Chairman, I would suggest to you that the Pension Act should be revised in such a way that the pensioner today would be at least on a level with those who are engaged in business or who are in the armed services. These figures show a disparity between the pension of the veteran and the pay of the armed forces as well as certain classes of civil servants. I put it to you, sir, that this disparity should not exist. I should like, in fact I would almost insist, that the disparity should not exist as between a man disabled as a result of war and those fellows who are capable of maintaining themselves.
These pensioners sacrificed all they had or hoped to have in the service of their country, and they should have a standard of living at least equal to the men and women of the armed forces. They do not have this today. By what process of mental calisthenics the official mind has arrived at these figures is something that is quite obscure. Historically, these pensions have been tied in with what one could receive in the labour market. The examples I have pointed out show you that today such a comparison is not applicable. During the years since 1920 the disparity has steadily widened. I would submit to you, Mr. Chairman, this condition should not have been allowed to develop and pension rates have failed to keep pace with wages in the services or in industry.
Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, I note that a widow is always expected to live on less than a single pensioner. Just why this should be so is not apparent to me. Why one single individual should be expected to live on less
Pension Act
than another single individual is something that is not quite apparent to me. Evidently this results from one of those peculiarities that exist in the official mind. Apparently the government can not grasp the fact that the war disability pension is a matter of contractual right and not a matter of charity. It is a moral obligation based on equity and should be looked on in that particular way because when we come to discharge this obligation, we are in a much different position than we are in so far as any other obligation we might assume is concerned, that is in regard to old age pensions or anything of that kind.
Then there is the question of the effective dates of the pensions. A man may have made an application for a pension three years ago and his pension may be granted today. However, there is no guarantee it is going to be retroactive to the date of the application. Why not? If a man is eligible for the pension now, then he should be eligible for it when he made application. He should therefore be in the position to collect for the difference in the length of time and should not be subjected to the loss of that pension merely because the pension board could not make up its mind.
Again I should like to point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that one of the features of the act that has always caused a great deal of discussion in veterans organizations has been this question of disability in a pensioner that was regarded as pre-enlistment, not aggravated. My own contention right along has been and still is that where a man has been accepted by the armed forces and has been passed by the examiners in those armed forces, that man is assumed to be in top medical condition-it is agreed that he is-and that if something else crops up during his service there must have been some degree of aggravation or it would not have cropped up. We therefore insist that, where a person was entitled to a clear medical sheet when he enlisted, anything that crops up subsequently during his service should be regarded as a disability created or aggravated by service.
Then again I notice that in these amendments no mention is made of any improvements with regard to orphans of veterans. They are not receiving a raise and they did not receive a raise last time.
There is another thing I wish to mention, namely the question of widows. While under these amendments the widow is being granted a raise the fact remains that if she happens to have a couple of children on her hands, those children are not subject to a raise. While the raise may and certainly

Pension Act
must be of value to the widow who is entitled to it, the fact remains that it is not going to help her a great deal if no raise is given to the children who are left under her care.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer you to Mr. Lapointe's attitude towards this matter at the last session of this house. That gentleman for a good many years was minister of veterans affairs in the previous government. I would commend his remarks to the present minister and suggest to him that the implications of those remarks are now in his hands. I hope that he will govern himself accordingly.

Mr. Chairman, I take it that the purpose of discussing this resolution is to enable the house to come to a decision as to whether the minister shall have leave to introduce a bill to amend the Canadian Pension Act. This would therefore appear to me to be a suitable opportunity to make a few observations so that the house may be informed as to how this act as at present administered applies to Newfoundland veterans. I particularly wish to bring this matter to the attention of the minister and his colleagues at this time in the hope that he may find it possible to include in his amendments some solution to the situations which I am about to describe.
Hon. members may have noticed that the province of Newfoundland is given the distinction of being the only province of Canada mentioned by name in the resolution now before the house. Since Newfoundland was supposed to have become a part of Canada in 1949, hon. members may like myself be wondering why it has been necessary to single out my province for this special mention. When Newfoundland joined Canada we all took it for granted that Newfoundland veterans would automatically become Canadian veterans and would be treated in every respect as though they had served in the Canadian forces. Very few veterans had access to copies of the terms of union at the time of confederation but most of us were supplied with a little booklet entitled, "Canada's Veterans Charter, How it Applies in the Province of Newfoundland". I should like to read a few short paragraphs of the introduction at page 4 of this booklet which was issued under the authority of the Hon. Milton F. Gregg, then minister of veterans affairs. The introduction on page 4 reads as follows:
This is a booklet addressed to Canada's newest veterans in the province of Newfoundland, those who in world war I and world war II fought so gallantly in the battles for freedom. The booklet is designed to inform you of those rights and privileges which you now have in common with your fellow-veterans who served from Canada.

Then follows the paragraph I wish to underline, Mr. Chairman:
Under the agreement for confederation the veteran who served from Newfoundland is in exactly the same position as those who served from the other nine provinces.
When we come to the terms of union we find that the rights and privileges of Newfoundland veterans are outlined in section 38. I do not intend to read the whole of this section but I think it would be helpful to hon. members if I put on the record the first two subsections. Section 38 of the terms of union is entitled "Veterans" and it reads in part as follows:
33. Canada will make available to Newfoundland veterans the following benefits, on the same basis as they are from time to time available to Canadian veterans, as if the Newfoundland veterans had served in His Majesty's Canadian forces, namely,
(a)	The War Veterans' Allowance Act, 1946, free hospitalization and treatment, and civil service preference will be extended to Newfoundland veterans who served in the first world war or the second world war or both;
(b)	Canada will assume as from the date of union the Newfoundland pension liability in respect of the first world war, and in respect of the second world war Canada will assume as from the date of union the cost of supplementing disability and dependants' pensions paid by the government of the United Kingdom or an allied country to Newfoundland veterans up to the level of the Canadian rates of pensions, and, in addition, Canada will pay pensions arising from disabilities that are pensionable under Canadian law but not pensionable either under the laws of the United Kingdom or under the laws of an allied country;
Then follow subsection (c) dealing with the Veterans' Land Act, subsection (d) dealing with re-establishment credit, subsection (e) dealing with vocational and educational training and subsection (f) covering the Veterans Rehabilitation Act.
In 1947, another official document was published entitled "Proposed Arrangements for the Entry of Newfoundland into Confederation". On page 11 of this document, war service benefits are outlined as annex 1 and I should like to read the first paragraph on that page:
Canada will extend to Newfoundland veterans who served with any of His Majesty's forces the following benefits on the same basis as if these Newfoundland veterans had served in His Majesty's Canadian forces . . .
Perhaps we were not justified in assuming that Newfoundland veterans would automatically become Canadian veterans upon confederation. In the face of the official statements I have just read, hon. members will have to decide this question for themselves. Whether we were justified or not, the fact remains that we did believe that on confederation we would be treated exactly as if we had served in the Canadian forces,

and when I say "we" I mean not only Newfoundland veterans but the Newfoundland public as well.
During the eight years that I have been a member of parliament I have had occasion to address a considerable number of letters to the Canadian pension commission dealing with the problems of Newfoundland veterans, and I must confess that I have often been puzzled by references in the replies I have received to the establishment of domiciliary residence in Newfoundland.
So firmly was the idea embedded in my mind that Newfoundland veterans upon confederation would be treated as if they had served in the Canadian forces that I must confess I was completely blind to the possibility that any other interpretation might be possible, and it was not until last year that it suddenly dawned upon me that not only were Newfoundland war veterans not regarded as Canadian veterans but that they were not even regarded as Newfoundland veterans, but as imperial veterans. That came as somewhat of a shock, because prior to confederation Newfoundland veterans had never regarded themselves as imperial veterans, nor were they so regarded by the Newfoundland government. It is true they served with the United Kingdom forces under United Kingdom command, but their identity was preserved by supplementary pay and allowances provided by the Newfoundland government, and on discharge their pensions also were supplemented by that government in accordance with a scale designed to bring them as far as possible in line with Canadian pensions.
I am not blaming anyone for this situation. I do not think it was done deliberately. I am not saying that the terms of union in this respect are incompatible with the interpretation which has been placed upon them. On the contrary, I have the highest regard for the personnel of the Canadian pension commission, as I have for the personnel of the war veterans allowance board and for the heads of the various branches of the Department of Veterans Affairs. But I say that I feel the interpretation which the Canadian pension commission is placing upon the Pension Act in its application to Newfoundland is not in accord with the spirit of the terms of union as expressed in the preamble to section 38 of the terms of union and in the booklet entitled "Canada's Veterans Charter".
I know it has been argued that the present arrangement works to the advantage of the Newfoundland veteran in that it gives him a choice of dealing either with the British ministry of pensions or with the Canadian pension commission; in other words, the Newfoundland veteran has two strings to his
Pension Act
bow and can choose the better of two possible worlds. I should like to reply to that argument now.
Canada's veterans charter has been described as the best and most generous in the whole world, and I believe every member of this house will subscribe to that view. But if that is true, as I believe it is, what advantage is there in being compelled to apply for the inferior British pension before being able to qualify for the more generous Canadian pension? If there is any advantage, I am unable to see it. I can, on the other hand, see a great many disadvantages. Hon. members will recall that section 38(b) of the confederation terms says that Canada will supplement the British pension up to Canadian rates.
Under this arrangement the Newfoundland veteran is, first of all, compelled to make his application to the British ministry of pensions. This means that the application must be forwarded to England to be adjudicated there, and the first disadvantage is the long delay while waiting for the application to travel back and forth and because of the time required by the British ministry of pensions to reach its decision. This process often takes weeks and it may even take several months. If the veteran concerned is incapacitated, or if his earning power is diminished by his incapacity, he and his family must exist all this while either on charity or on government relief, which constitutes a hardship which increases in severity as the period is prolonged.
In dealing with the application, the officials of the British ministry of pensions might arrive at one of three decisions. They might admit entitlement and grant a pension based on a percentage assessment of disability. In the second place they might grant entitlement and assess the disability as nil or, thirdly, they might reject the application altogether.
If the application is rejected outright the Newfoundland veteran then has the privilege of applying to the Canadian pension commission in which case he must begin all over again with still further delay and still more loss of time and prolonged hardship. If the British ministry of pensions grants entitlement but assesses the disability as nil, the veteran may find himself worse off than if his application had been rejected outright because he cannot then benefit from the supplementary provisions of the Canadian Pension Act even though, by Canadian standards, he might have an assessable degree of disability. The very fact the British ministry did not reject his claim debars him from taking advantage of section 13 (7) of the act even though his claim might easily be established under Canadian law and assessed under the Canadian table of disabilities.

Pension Act
I am not able to follow the mathematical reasoning of the Canadian pension commission in taking this stand. When I went to school I learned that zero plus one equalled one, and that zero plus ten equalled ten and that zero could be supplemented in any degree by adding whatever digit to it you wished to add. All I can say is that if the Russian scientists and mathematicians had adopted the new mathematical law formulated by the Canadian pension commission we would not have to worry today about sputniks travelling around over our heads. In any case the present situation where a veteran whose claim for a pension is rejected is better off than one whose claim is admitted is a bit ridiculous, to say the least, and I urge the minister to take whatever steps lie in his power to have it changed.
Should the British ministry of pensions grant a pension the Canadian pension commission will, as I just said, supplement the British pension under section 13 (7) of the act with an amount that will bring it up to Canadian standards but even then the present supplementary provisions of the Canadian Pension Act fail to provide complete coverage even for those who, in the main, qualify for supplementation, because should the Newfoundland pensioner who is in receipt of supplementation, or his dependants, subsequently take up residence outside of Canada they immediately lose the supplementation and revert back to British rates. This result gives rise to a most peculiar situation in that a veteran wounded in action whose claim is granted by the British and supplemented by the Canadian pension commission loses his supplementation if he leaves Canada. The same thing is true as far as his widow and dependants are concerned. Should the widow find it necessary to go and live with a daughter in the United States or anywhere outside of Canada she loses the benefit of the supplementation but on the other hand the veteran who never left Newfoundland during service or whose claim having been rejected by the British is established directly under section 13 (7) is paid at Canadian rates as a matter of right and he and his widow and dependants can go anywhere in the world without losing the supplementation. This is not only ridiculous, it is totally contrary to the spirit of the terms of union and it is not in accord with official statements which have been made concerning Newfoundland veterans.
One other serious complaint that Newfoundland veterans have is the long time between appeal board hearings. The last hearing of the appeal board in Newfoundland was held last September and the one before

that was held in April 1956. The long interval between hearings of the appeal board is not only a poor service to the veterans of Newfoundland but a cause of great inconvenience since some appellants are compelled to wait as long as 15 months before their cases are heard.
According to the Canadian pension commission the Pension Act does not make provision for payment of widows pensions as of right to those widows whose husbands were in receipt of 50 per cent or more pension at the time of their death if death occurred prior to April 1, 1949. Although these widows have been provided for from a special fund they have not been automatically granted the last two pension increases and I should like the minister to pay special attention to this matter and see what can be done to ensure that these widows will receive their benefits as a matter of right the same as do widows of veterans who serve in the Canadian forces.

Perhaps I might just interrupt for a moment, Mr. Chairman, to assure the hon. member that we will take into very careful consideration the points he has raised; but I do express my amazement at the fact that this is the first time the hon. member, who has been in this house since confederation, ever brought this to the attention of the House of Commons. It is very amazing to me.
Mr. Chairman, I explained to the committee why it was we did not bring it up before.
Oh, oh.
It did not dawn upon us before.
Oh, oh.
We took for granted what the veterans charter said.
You made a big mistake there.
And we took for granted what the terms of union said. I will read that section to the minister again if he wishes to have his memory refreshed.
The hon. member need not read the terms of union to me. He has been complaining that his government did not take this into consideration.
I am not complaining at all nor am I blaming anybody for this, but I am pointing out to the minister that this situation does exist now and it is one that should not be allowed to continue further.
I agree with the hon. member.
The government has improved the situation.

These amendments will not represent any improvement as far as these problems are concerned. I hope that when the minister brings in his legislation it will be drafted in such a way as to provide a satisfactory solution to the problems I have outlined. In fact, my purpose in speaking now rather than on second reading is to acquaint the minister with these problems so he can see whether something can be done in terms of finding a solution.
The reason we were blinded and it took us so long to realize what the present situation actually is was the ambiguity of section 38 of the terms of union of Newfoundland with Canada. This section reads:
Canada will make available to Newfoundland veterans the following benefits, on the same basis as they are from time to time available to Canadian veterans, as if the Newfoundland veterans had served in His Majesty's Canadian forces-
I would point out that the Newfoundland veterans are not being treated as though they had served in His Majesty's Canadian forces but rather as though they had served in His Majesty's imperial forces.
It certainly took you a long time to realize that.
That may be, but better late than never; and the minister and the commission will now have no further excuse for delaying action to correct the situation.
We are just working harder than the other opposition.
What excuse do you make for your own government?

I wish to bring to the minister's attention the fact that the wording of the present Canadian pension life certificate, CPC-103, is misleading in regard to children over 16 and 17 who are attending school or who may be incapacitated mentally or physically. I have come in contact with several cases of pensioners who did not know they could claim additional pension for their children up to the age of 21 as long as such children continued to make satisfactory progress in school and I would be grateful if something could be done to clarify the wording of that particular clause.
Finally, I should like to point out to the minister I have been informed that there is a precedent in the department which, if it were adopted, would alleviate all of the problems to which I have just referred. I can understand that distinction would be made between a veteran who deliberately by-passed the Canadian forces and went and enlisted in the forces of another country. I can understand that such a veteran would not have the same claim as a veteran who did not by-pass those forces; but that does
Pension Act
not apply to Newfoundland veterans. We did not by-pass the Canadian forces; we had no other choice at the time. I understand that during the war an occasion occurred when it was necessary for a number of the Canadian air force personnel to be transferred to the British air force. I am not familiar with the complete details, but I understand that in the case of those veterans special treatment was given. In other words, this particular group of veterans was not treated as though they had by-passed the Canadian forces to join the imperial forces. If that same reasoning could be applied to the Newfoundland veterans most of our problems could be worked out and I heartily commend this to the minister's attention.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate, I have no intention of delaying the adoption of the resolution now before us. Rather do I wish to say how pleased the veterans of this country have been with these amendments to the various pieces of pension legislation which are of special concern to them.
Like so many other younger members, especially those who sit on this side of the house, I am a veteran. Thanks to Providence I came out of the war without any wounds or illness. However, thousands of my comrades have had a different fate, and it is up to us to see to it that they receive an adequate pension. I think that the adoption of the amendments which are being discussed this afternoon, and which in any case will be considered for several days, will help us achieve our aim, that of granting these men an equitable pension.
(Text):
I would like to say only a few words, Mr. Chairman, as one of those in this house who is a veteran and perhaps among the luckier veterans who came out of world war I or world war II without any wounds, any disabilities and I hope no lasting illnesses. I merely say that we as Canadians owe to these men who offered themselves as volunteers in the defence of this and other countries a great deal; that we should help them to maintain a decent standard of living by affording them some measure of pension.
Like many members on both sides of the house I, too, feel that we can go a long way yet to achieve the ideal pension scheme. Notwithstanding what may have been said by others, I look to the early setting up of a permanent committee on veterans affairs to investigate our whole pension scheme and all matters related to veterans affairs. However, I do not agree that at this moment we should

Pension Act
have held off the early consideration of these emergent matters for the purpose of going into a long and careful study of the subject. I am sure hon. members will agree that it is not something that can be decided or investigated within the confines of a week or two. It will require representations and investigations on all sides if we are to achieve what we believe to be the ideal, and I feel that great injustice would have been done by adopting a long procedure.
We have before us what are considered to be very distressing conditions, as the Canadian Legion has pointed out for many years. I come from Edmonton where I do have the support of a great number of the members of the Canadian Legion. Edmonton is proud of the fact that its principal branch, the Montgomery branch, is the largest branch of the Canadian Legion in this country. In addition, we have two other branches, so it is not an isolated movement in Alberta and in Edmonton in particular.
Following the observations of some hon. members, I would say that I have some reservations on the point advanced by the Legion and by hon. members in this house that pensions should be tied in to the scale of pay of the services. It must be remembered that the scale of pay of the services is tied in closely with the competitive labour market. I do not think the same parallel exists between the pension and the competitive labour field. With that, Mr. Chairman, I would say that I am prepared, along with many other hon. members, to support the general principles of this bill.

Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to see how bipartisan the veterans policy is. Like most hon. members, I too am a veteran and in the past I have been very proud of the part that the Department of Veterans Affairs has played in the welfare of our returned people. On most occasions it has been bipartisan, and we are pleased to see that it is so today. Of course, I think a committee could be set up to study veterans' affairs. I do not think the fact that we pass this legislation will take away the need for setting up such a committee to discuss further the problems of veterans that are not settled by this resolution.
I should like to congratulate Mr. Burgess, the dominion president of the Canadian Legion, on the presentation that they made and the able manner in which the work has been done which has gone into that presentation.
In my particular area the Canadian Legion has always played a prominent part in veterans affairs. From my reading of the

brief and from the knowledge that I have of veterans problems-it may be small-I think the Minister of Veterans Affairs might have given more consideration to increasing the amounts which are being increased to bring them up to the 33i per cent which has been asked for by the Canadian Legion. At all times I have found the Legion moderate in the extreme. They have always tended to be on the conservative side, with a small "c". At no time have their demands been anything other than reasonable.
I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that at the present time there are people working in the House of Commons who are veterans of the British armed forces. When they applied for jobs here they were instructed that they did not come under the veterans preference. That is a matter that could be taken into consideration and perhaps some thought given to it.
I have found on many occasions that persons reporting to the pension board for their annual check-up-I have been in that position myself-have been instructed by the doctors sitting on the board and dealing with the review of pension cases that they have looked in the files and found no entries, no medical evidence that the pensioner had needed attention since the last time they saw him. I think some consideration should be given to this problem in those instances where medical plans are in operation. A doctor may be working continuously in an area under a medical plan and in many cases he does not see fit to fill out the forms for the Department of Veterans Affairs. Therefore, even though the man may be treated once a week, once a month or at irregular intervals, there is no record of such treatment, and when he comes before the board for the annual review there is no record of any medical service having been given to that particular pensioner. The obvious conclusion drawn from the blank record for that year is that he has not needed any treatment.
I am not sure what amount doctors are paid for calls involving pensioners but it may be that the rate is not sufficiently high to warrant the doctor filling out the form. He may find it is much more profitable to use the medical plan in that particular area.
There are also a number of cases, including one in particular about which I can speak with some authority, where the veteran comes before a pension board in a small community and there are no specialists attached to the review board with the result that the pensioner is sent somewhere else to see a specialist. In some cases I think the pensioner is legitimately justified in saying that when he is sent to a private practitioner

he should only be sent there for examination and should not be compelled to take treatment, treatment that would only serve to put a few dollars in the pocket of the particular specialist and would have no bearing whatsoever on the pension review being undertaken.
In the particular case I have in mind the person's pension was cut because he had refused the treatment, and he had simply been sent to the specialist for an examination and not for treatment. If these matters are brought to the minister's attention I am quite sure he will take cognizance of them and it will not be necessary to say any more about them.
On occasion we have had problems with a type of veteran who does not appear to be covered by the Department of Veterans Affairs Act. There are a number, some of whom I know personally, who served in the merchant navy, saw action and were wounded by shells or torpedoes and are unable to get any type of pension. It seems that originally there was a pension for merchant seamen and that when the war began that pension was discontinued. A period of time elapsed before the pension plan under which they were then brought was put into effect. One particular chap I know lost an arm and was badly shot up, but there is no coverage for him. I believe this matter has been raised in the house on a number of occasions. This person has never received any pension, and I think it can be legitimately argued that he was serving in a very active field of hostilities.
In talking to soldiers, airmen and navy personnel recently I was most surprised to find that they do not come under what we would have considered the protection of the Department of Veterans Affairs while we were service personnel. It is true that while they are on duty for their eight hours a day they would be covered in case of accidents when working at the job they are supposed to be doing. I am not going to repeat a number of cases that have been mentioned. There was one discussed at some length in 1956, an accident where a man was killed while still under the orders of his superior officer. But because what he was doing was considered to be outside the line of duty his wife received no pension.
However, it would appear to me that in such cases we could reasonably ask the government to provide and pay for an insurance plan that would at least supply some of the necessities for the widows and dependants of these service personnel who at the present time are serving their country not only in Canada but in foreign lands. It does not
Pension Act
appear to me that there would be much satisfaction involved for some lady, whose husband had been killed on the streets of Paris, being told that he was not on duty at that particular time and that nothing could be done about it. There has always been a certain honour and pride in serving in the forces of Canada and I think we should protect that at least with insurance which would cover these people in the hours when they are considered not to be working. I think that rates could be arranged whereby insurance of $20,000 or $25,000 would not be prohibitive in cost and I believe such a move would be very favourably received by the armed services.
Finally, I should like to leave the thought with the minister that some consideration be given to setting aside November 11 as a national holiday. Every person in Canada has had some close friend or relative who gave their life in the service of Canada. Indeed, many of us have had hundreds. The least I think we can do for them is to set aside one day on which to honour their memory.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be confined to the difficulties that pensioners encounter in having their medical condition reviewed and given what they consider is proper attention. It is not unusual for a veteran to find after appealing a decision that the same members are sitting on the court of appeal as were on the original examination board. I think all members will agree that is not a fair practice. Generally, pensioners have found that once a negative decision is made by an appeal board or by an examining board, as the case may be, it is almost impossible to have the decision changed or modified despite any evidence from local or family doctors that may be presented.
I am going to deal with a couple of cases for which I can vouch personally, and the information I am going to give the house is on record. There is a veteran not too far from my home town who suffered gunshot wounds in 1918. Shortly after being treated in hospital he was demobilized in the last year of the war and had only been home a short time when he became crippled with sciatica. This was in 1919. Since that time, Mr. Chairman, we have a continuous record of sciatica and suffering on the part of this veteran. At various stages during those years he was completely disabled. We have references here to statements by local doctors. I am going to read a recommendation that was made by Dr. Meekison in 1935. This is his opinion:
This man is totally disabled with bilateral severe sciatic neuritis. In the absence of other causes.

Pension Act
it is very reasonable to assume that his present condition is due to his gunshot wounds. Something should be done for this man.
We can go back a little bit earlier to 1919. This veteran was discharged and took up residence on Vancouver island. Suffering, and totally disabled as he was, he went to various doctors in his own neighbourhood and on the mainland. Finally, he was advised to seek another climate and he moved to Kamloops in the interior of British Columbia. From there, he moved a little farther westward and now is residing very close to my home town. From 1918 until the present time this man has been continuously suffering from sciatica. Various family doctors and local doctors have agreed on this man's condition. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that their opinions are just as worthy of consideration as any specialist who might sit on a board that the veterans affairs department might set up. I maintain that these opinions should be given some consideration in trying to reach a solution of this case. This example is forcibly in my mind at the present time because I have just taken it up with the pension commission in Ottawa. This morning I received a letter which does not make me feel too happy. I am not going to read the letter, Mr. Chairman, because it is rather lengthy. However, the last paragraph says this:
He is a veteran with a good record of service, and possibly would qualify for reinstatement on war veterans' allowance if he is no longer gainfully employed.
I say that if he is not employed and is entitled to war veterans' allowance then, in the face of the facts set out in this brief, he is entitled to a straight disability pension. In view of this, we feel the case should be reopened and he should receive more serious consideration.
I am going to mention one more case, Mr. Chairman. A young lad left school in 1944 to go into the armed forces of this country. He took his infantry training and was sent to Germany with the army of occupation. He had no active service, through no fault of his own. On discharge from the army he was examined by the medical officer and put in category F. Hon. members know this meant automatic attention by the pension board. The reason for placing him in this category was a severe heart condition. Within a short time he was called to Vancouver for examination before the board, and the board said there was absolutely nothing wrong with him. A few short weeks before that the army examining officer had placed him in category F and had made a remark-these are his exact words and therefore I would
like to have them on the record-"How in hell did you ever go through the army training?"
In spite of this, within a few short weeks the appeal board said there was nothing wrong with him; he had a perfect heart and was in perfect physical condition. I know this lad. I know that even today, after all these years, he has to be careful of the kind of employment he accepts. He cannot engage in sports. He cannot engage in any physical activity beyond that necessary to move in a very quiet occupation. If he cuts his own lawn, within a few minutes you will find him stretched out on a couch resting; that is the kind of lad the medical board said was in perfect physical condition.
These are examples that I think should be given a little more serious attention. There is something wrong when people such as these two I have mentioned feel it is hopeless to request that their case be reviewed. This lad who was discharged in 1946 is convinced it is hopeless to try to do anything about the decision of the board. From the evidence I have here, and from speaking to so many veterans in similar circumstances, I am inclined to agree that it is almost hopeless to try to have a case re-opened and get a decision that has once been in the negative reversed.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take much of the time of the house this afternoon. In fact, I had not intended to say anything at all but I am taking part in the debate because of certain remarks that have been made. I might say that I am very sympathetic towards the cases cited by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, as well as the other grievances that have been raised this afternoon. I believe they will receive attention and correction. I believe these hon. members put forth a genuine effort in putting their cases before the committee. On the other hand, the submissions made by the hon. member for Rosthern as well as the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount are in a different position altogether.
While these hon. members were in favour of this measure, they could go along with it, they introduced the promises made by the leader of the government and stated he had not lived up to those promises. They felt the Prime Minister had not lived up to his promises because the pensions were not related to a formula tied to the gross national product of this country or the rising cost of living. The hon. member for Rosthern also made the point that our leader had not lived up to his promises in regard to this legislation because it had not been brought into effect immediately.

As I listened to both these hon. members I thought they sounded like a lawyer who comes into court with a very bad case. He has nothing to work with. So he is obliged to go into great fulminations, with great fury and furor, in an effort to try to distract the judge or the jury from the weakness of his case. This is the simple proposition with which the house is confronted.
They have now found that the leader of the government is living up to every one of the promises he has made and the people of this country have great faith in him. That is the reason they are an aggregation of Ishmalites. They found we have "Honest John" who is delivering the goods. They themselves are surprised, in view of the tortoise-like movement which the previous government had. Now they go into kangaroolike activity and say that this thing must be done overnight.
Let me tell you the people of Canada certainly placed their confidence in the right man. He is giving them the legislation and is fulfilling his promises with an alacrity that has dumbfounded the official opposition. I am not a bit surprised that the hon. member for Rosthern, when speaking the other night, said that he was amazed at some of the legislation that came in. We were amazed at his amazement. However, while they have a very weak case and they are now trying strenuously to find a way out, it is certainly amusing.
After this goes on for a few more weeks, the people of Canada will discern just exactly what they are trying to do. They will discern that they are trying to develop a case to go to the people saying, "We are now going to do something for you", notwithstanding the fact that it took them nearly 39 years to bring in their health legislation that had been promised continuously since 1919. They brought down an omnibus piece of legislation last March that covered the veterans assistance. It was nebulous. It did not have anything tied in with it and it left the government of today in a position to find the money to finance it.
However, I would say this. There is a certain amount of amusement in the situation. It brings to mind the comment once made by Patrick Henry: "How the mighty have fallen". Then I should like to wind up with a quotation from holy writ. When Eli was disturbed at the progress of the battle with the Phil-listines in which his two sons were engaged; they had not prepared for the fray and the armies were in no condition to fulfil what Israel expected of them, he died from the shock of Israel's defeat, and his two sons died in the battle. The wife of Eli's son Phineas
Pension Act
was great with child and expected soon. When the child was born, because of the calamitous defeat of Israel and his fathers part in it, she in her sorrow named it Ichabod, which means thy glory has faded. That is the condition in which the Liberal party now finds itself.

I have just a brief word to say, Mr. Chairman. I listened to the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke state the two cases with which he had difficulty. The reason why I rose is that I also had a case with which I had difficulty. I can advise the hon. member to take the same course as I took and he will not be sorry. This veteran to whom I refer had been thrown from the top of a lorry and lit on the hard road on his back. He was never able to walk very well after that time. After some years his walking ability became worse and worse and he was badly crippled. What 1 did was what I think any hon. member ought to do. I placed the case before the chairman of the pension board. I gave him particulars. In less than three months the man had a 100 per cent pension. I would advise any hon. member to do just what has been done today. I would advise him to get the particulars and give them to the chairman of the pension board. Then the doctors will be obliged to prove their cases.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to delay the house more than a couple of minutes at this stage but when my genial friend the hon. member for Danforth spoke, he made a comment about which I could not refrain from making some observations. He spoke about what was done last spring as being very nebulous. I just wish to draw to his attention the fact that what we did last spring was to increase the amount paid to the single veteran by $25 a month and that to the married pensioner by $30 a month. This increase went to all pensioners. If, in his opinion, that is nebulous, Mr. Chairman, then how much more nebulous is this bill which does not increase the basic pensions at all.
I give credit to the minister for being quite straightforward with the house in saying that he is not proposing to increase the basic pensions at all in this legislation. That makes it extremely difficult to understand why, for example, the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond seemed to think that this legislation was going to increase basic pensions. I was sorry he did not consult some of the leaders and some of the experienced members of his party who would have set him right on the matter. In fact, I am surprised that he should have said it at all when the minister was so clear in stating that the only way in which basic pensions would be affected by this legislation would be to incorporate in the bill what is already law-in other words these

Pension Act
increases that were made last spring are now the law-and put it in the Pension Act. The minister was quite trank about that matter. I think anybody who is supporting this legislation with the idea that it is increasing the basic pensions should have listened more closely to what the minister said quite honestly in speaking to the resolution.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister a question. This concerns how decisions are arrived at concerning entitlement. It an applicant was accepted into any branch of the armed services as being in category A and is later discharged as being in a lower category, can the pension board disclaim responsibility on the ground that the health condition which led to discharge existed previously to enlistment?

Mr. Chairman, the question which is asked by the hon. member will be dealt with when we are discussing the bill. We are at the resolution stage now.
Having listened to the observations made by hon. members, I may say that I am pleased to have the suggestions that many of them have made. The many points which have been referred to me will be given careful consideration and when we are discussing second reading of this bill, I shall be pleased indeed to deal with them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?

Mr. Chairman, before I come to the matters I wish to develop I should like to ask the minister if he would give some thought to the question of the Canadian firefighters. It would, I think, be a good thing for him to examine the whole subject, to find out how many firefighters went overseas from Canada, when they went, how long they were overseas and what was the nature of the dangers they encountered; how many casualties they suffered and whether or not some consideration should be given them in order to reward them for the good work they did to assist Great Britain in the days of the war when fires were very widespread and very hard to put out.
I have listened with a good deal of thought and attention to the speeches made by the various hon. members who have taken part in the debate. I believe that if I were a reader of Hansard out in the country I should find it difficult to get an over-all picture of the situation which confronts Canada in respect of the veterans.
I thought that the submission which has recently been placed in the hands of the Prime Minister by the Canadian Legion was about as fine a thing as I have read on the whole subject. In my opinion it would be valuable to the people in the country who

read Hansard, not now, but in the future and who might bring matters before succeeding governments if we listed the recommendations contained in this submission. I should like to commend the man who drew up this brief. Already there have been a number of comments with respect to the conservative, moderate tone one finds throughout the submission and the moderate nature of the demands it contains. I should like to commend the author myself. On page 1, I read this statement which, I believe, is an important one:
In the light of this exceedingly serious situation and of world tensions today, we urge that there will be no unwarranted cutback in our defence budget and expenditures. Instead, this is a time fcr renewed and accelerated effort.
All hon. members will, I believe, support this idea, though as far as I have heard, no hon. member has supported it in the speech he made either before the committee or the house. On page 3 of the submission we read this:
The Canadian Legion therefore recommends

that manpower and equipment for the defence of Canada be maintained and extended according to the exigencies and requirements of NATO and the United Nations and our obligations to them; that the government does not reduce defence expenditure except in cases where the national safety be not impaired by so doing; and that the government shall adopt a policy in which the primary consideration shall be the fullest development of the best brains of Canada for purposes of defence by subsidizing higher education and scientific research in centres of learning in Canada.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. I dislike very much interrupting the hon. member, but we are discussing the Department of Veterans Affairs. The subject matter which he is dealing with now has nothing to do with the Department of Veterans Affairs but is entirely the responsibility of the Department of National Defence, which is probably the reason why none of the other hon. members discussed it this afternoon.
Mr. Chairman, I have just finished that part of my remarks. But I think we cannot stress this important matter too much, even though we are dealing only with veterans affairs-
Yes, at the proper time.

Industrial Relations
provide the goods and services necessary to establish a high standard of living for her soldiers we find there is everything in Canada but the common sense necessary to make what is physically possible financially possible. Therefore, I think the people of this country ought to be aroused to the point where they will say, "Look here, if we can produce all the milk and other products of that kind to provide for our population and all the goods and services necessary to provide a comfortable standard of living, it is downright scandalous if our veterans cannot be provided with all of those things they need and can use".
I thought it would be worth while, Mr. Chairman, just to say a few words along this line. I have not said very much concerning veterans affairs during the last few years because we have had very able spokesmen in this group and because as it has been organized it has not been my particular responsibility to speak on the subject of veterans affairs. Nor is it my special responsibility today except that as a representative of the constituency of Lethbridge in which there are great numbers of veterans from world war I and world war II and a number from the Korean war I feel that it now becomes my duty to the veterans and the people of Lethbridge generally to speak out in support of a better deal for the veteran all across the board.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Brooks thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 35, to amend the Pension Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

subtopic: PROVISION OP ANNUAL VACATIONS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL WORKS

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Starr (Minister of Labour) moved
subtopic: PROVISION OP ANNUAL VACATIONS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL WORKS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 16, to provide for annual vacations with pay for employees in public works, undertakings and businesses.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I rise in moving second reading of Bill No. 16 which is an act to provide for annual vacations with pay for employees in federal works, undertakings and businesses I consider it a great privilege for me to be able to present this bill to the house at this time. I hope that in days to come I will have the privilege of presenting other bills which will be of benefit to the people of Canada.
The purpose of this bill is quite simple. It aims to provide two weeks annual vacation with pay to all employees who have

completed two years' employment in industries under federal jurisdiction and one
week's holiday with pay for those who have completed less than two years, but at least one year. In the first instance, pay is calculated at 4 per cent of the gross earnings, and in the second instance at 2 per cent. The bill provides an answer to many requests which have been put forward over the years by labour unions and other interested groups and, in effect, grants what has customarily been a subject of collective bargaining. It takes the two weeks vacation out of the collective bargaining arena and makes it mandatory for employees with more than two years' service.
This legislation will benefit employees in works and undertakings connected with shipping, navigation, railways, canals, telegraphs and other interprovincial and extra-provincial activities, including ferries, aircraft, radio broadcasting, banks and one or two industries such as uranium which have been declared by parliament to be for the general advantage of Canada. The act also applies to crown corporations.
A majority of employees in these industries are now getting two-week vacations as a result of collective bargaining agreements. However, there are still approximately 5,000 workers in these industries who do not receive vacations with pay as a matter of right. Furthermore, there are more than 150,000 workers in these fields who must be employed for three years before qualifying for two weeks holidays with pay as outlined in this proposed measure.
In arriving at the provisions of the present bill we felt it necessary to study the provincial legislation in this field. Five provinces provide for a vacation of one week after one year, they are New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta; two provinces provide for a vacation of two weeks after one year, namely Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Alberta also provides for two weeks' vacation after two years and Manitoba provides for two weeks after three years. Thus it can be seen that Bill No. 16 is equal to or better than the vacations provided in five of the seven provinces having this legislation. There is no provincial vacation legislation in Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. The New Brunswick legislation applies only to mining, construction and related industries brought within the scope of the act by Order in Council.
As to the various features of the bill, I feel that it compares favourably with any such legislation elsewhere. A year of employment is reckoned from the day on which

continuous employment begins. There is also provision for a vacation plan based on a calendar year system, which is subject to certain conditions which will be set out in regulations. Thus, the bill will be quite flexible in its application.
The period within which the employer is required to schedule the vacation is set at 10 months following the anniversary day marking the completion of the year of employment. This is the period commonly fixed in legislation in the provinces.
Should a holiday occur during vacation- such as July 1 or Labour day-the vacation is extended by one day with pay provided that the employee would have been paid for working on that day had he not been on vacation. A transfer of business to a new owner does not break continuity of employment.
When the legislation comes into effect all those who have completed the required period of continuous employment will be entitled to the stipulated holidays with pay, as detailed in the bill.
On termination of employment an employee is entitled to vacation for any completed year in which he has not received a vacation and also for the completed portion of the year, based on two per cent, or four per cent, depending on the period of service. This does not apply if employment is less than 30 days duration.
The legislation overrides any other contract or arrangement except when such contract or arrangement is more favourable to the employee. A collective bargaining agreement, however, is an exception if it is binding upon the employer when this legislation comes into force. If the agreement provides for an annual vacation, the terms of the agreement shall continue to prevail until the agreement runs out. This will make for orderly adoption of the legislation and prevent confusion.
The legislation provides authority to make regulations dealing with administrative and enforcement matters. There is also authority to make special provisions in respect of seasonal or temporary employees.
I feel that these provisions, Mr. Speaker, should commend themselves to the house and that this legislation is a positive step toward giving labour as a statutory right what has long been a subject of bargaining.

subtopic: PROVISION OP ANNUAL VACATIONS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I wish to compliment the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) on his very worth-while contribution this afternoon and on the way in which he has explained the provisions of the bill which he proposes, which
Industrial Relations
will provide for vacations with pay for all of those employees who come within the jurisdiction of the federal government. It has always been my contention that matters such as these should not necessarily be left to the collective bargaining table. During my years of support of the Liberal administration I have worked ardently in an endeavour to get the cabinet to see my way of thinking, not only with regard to this particular measure, but with regard to union security and other legislation which might be of benefit to labour itself and to the labour movement in general. Therefore, I do not think it is inconsistent on my part to congratulate the minister on his introduction of this bill and again on the very clear manner in which he explained its various details.
I do think, however, that the minister should have given consideration to the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) which does provide better legislation, in that an employee after working one year would be entitled to two weeks holidays with pay. After all, that employee during the year has contributed an equal amount to the industry itself, to the production of the industry and to the profit that that industry might show.
I find it difficult to understand why the government should wish to discriminate between one year of service and two years of service. If the minister intends to use length of service as a yardstick for vacations with pay then he should take the matter further, as some corporations do, and give extra holidays for continuing service. That is all I have to say on this point.
I am pleased to note that it does extend to crown corporations. While the minister has said that the majority of those employed in crown corporations already enjoy the benefits of vacations with pay, he has indicated that there are some 5,000 not now receiving vacations with pay. This legislation is certainly going to be helpful to them.
It is quite revealing to hear that 150,000 employees must work three years before receiving two weeks vacation. The federal government, which is the senior government, and which has in the past in many respects been very progressive, should be the one to take the lead in all of these matters. Therefore, I think the minister in drafting this legislation should follow the pattern of some of the provinces which do have legislation which is much better than this bill. I believe the minister did say-and I know it to be a fact-that the province of British Columbia provides for two weeks holidays with pay and, of course, that extends not only to employees of the government or corporations

Industrial Relations
coming under its jurisdiction, but to everyone. We should use that as a yardstick. I would hope that when the minister introduces the bill and we come to that particular clause he will be prepared to move an amendment which will have the effect of removing any apparent discrimination.
I am pleased to note also that when a statutory holiday falls within a vacation period the employee will be allowed one extra day of vacation and will be paid for the extra day. This follows the practice of the more progressive industries, and I am pleased to note that the minister has adopted that policy. I am pleased to note also, although it is not too important, that there will not be too much confusion with respect to collective agreements that are already in effect. I have little more to say. I welcome the legislation and I am sure that everyone on this side of the house will give the minister all the support necessary.

subtopic: PROVISION OP ANNUAL VACATIONS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL WORKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member who has just spoken I should like to offer my congratulations to the minister on the manner in which he introduced the bill and dealt with some of the more technical aspects of it. I certainly cannot go as far as the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) and give complete endorsa-tion to the provisions contained in the bill. In fact, when I read a copy of the bill and studied it I debated in my own mind whether it would be advantageous to vote for it because there are certainly a number of deficiencies in the proposal now before us.
In my opinion, one major one is that the bill reveals a different attitude on the part of the people occupying the government benches now from that which they expressed in 1956 when a similar bill was before the house and was voted on. I note that on July 27, 1956, ten of the present cabinet ministers stood up in the house in their places and voted in favour of a bill which contained far better provisions than this one does. Perhaps at some later date we can have an explanation of why this change of mind has taken place.
There is another matter which I think is not too good. While it does not relate specifically to the bill, nevertheless I hope, Mr. Speaker, that you will grant me the leeway to deal with it. We have understood for some time that the Conservative party-this was enunciated quite strongly in some quarters during the election campaign-was in favour of a unified national labour code or uniformity of legislation throughout Canada. I would have been far more pleased if the minister had been able to introduce a bill and make the necessary changes in other legislation under our

jurisdiction that would have provided a uniform system of vacation allowances and payment therefor in all of the provinces of Canada and the Northwest Territories so as to cover all the people who at present come under the labour jurisdiction of this parliament. We would have been far better off. We could have approached the provinces along these lines and have moved towards establishing a uniform labour code by taking the first step on the question of vacations rather than adding just another system to the five or six, I think the minister said, in those provinces with vacation with pay legislation.
In my opinion, there are many other things wrong about the bill presented to us. I hope we will be able to take the opportunity at another stage of the proceedings on the bill to deal with them more particularly and to get clearer answers from the minister about them. I hope to convince him that the suggestions we will make with respect to certain clauses are valid and that they will be accepted.
Many hon. members who have been here for some years will know that the members of the present government, when they sat on the other side of the house, complained regularly, bitterly and justifiably so, I think, about too much legislation by order in council and not enough by parliament. We heard all about the supremacy of parliament in deciding these things. Yet when we look at the bill now before us we find that it makes provision for regulations which could very easily and conceivably end by being longer than the legislation itself. I for one am opposed to giving that amount of authority to make regulations under this legislation especially when there is provision for putting some extra loopholes in the regulations, exempting certain groups of people from the legislation and similar things of that nature. All that the bill does, if we accept the minister's figures as to the number of people who will be covered by the legislation, and I do accept them, is to go about halfway in effecting statutory recognition of certain rights which have been obtained through collective bargaining.
There is another point in which I am interested and I hope the minister will take the opportunity to answer regarding it. It relates again to what we understood to be the policy of the government as enunciated during the election campaign in the matter of drafting and enacting so-called labour legislation, of which this is a piece. We understood that the legislation would be drafted after consultation and discussion between labour and management groups so that all would be present at one time to

present their ideas and views, I do not know whether or not it has been done. If it has, then to my knowledge it has not been very well publicized and not too many people know anything about it other than the presentation which was made to the government by the Canadian Labour Congress.
Not only in this parliament but in the
legislatures of the various provinces where there are governments that are partial to what I might classify as the present capitalist system we invariably see that when legislation is drafted by a government following that type of thinking the legislation generally reflects the attitude of the Canadian Manufacturers Association and does not represent too well the desires and needs of the working classes. If legislation does err or is flexible in any way, it errs or is flexible so far as the employer is concerned and is not flexible with respect to the people who will receive benefits under such legislation.
If I have got the wrong impression from some of the words the minister used, I beg his forgiveness, but I understood him to say that the bill would take the question of vacations with pay out of the realm of collective bargaining. I do not see that in the bill. I do not think that is what the minister meant to imply. I hope I have got the wrong impression because I certainly would not want to see anything take place that would remove anything relating to collective bargaining from that process. Certainly the people who join unions want to see their unions get for them the best possible wages, hours and working conditions by collective bargaining and in contractual provisions with their employer. I hope I got the wrong impression from what the minister said.
Perhaps at this stage we could conclude by saying that while we do not wholeheartedly endorse all the provisions contained in the bill we are in agreement with the general principle of providing vacations with pay for employees. There is plenty of precedent for it in the various provinces that have passed legislation establishing vacations with pay for employees under their jurisdiction, and we have just followed that. When the bill reaches another stage I shall have more criticism and suggestions to make for changes to plug the loopholes that exist in this bill.

speechtext:
It is not
my purpose at this time to go into the details of the bill. When the question of introducing this bill came up the other day I did not think it was definitely established we would go on with it today. I should like to say to the minister that I think the introduction of
Industrial Relations
this legislation is very timely. It is something which we in the Social Credit party have always advocated, that is that the working man should be entitled to at least two weeks' vacation with pay in any one year. This is the first time that the government has come forward with a bill to make it known definitely by legislation that all those employees in the federal field would be receiving this benefit.
In so far as the reference to taking the matter out of collective bargaining is concerned, it does seem to me that once this bill becomes law then all those people employed in government corporations, such as the C.B.C., the railways, those working on government ships and things of that kind, will have the right to have two weeks' vacation with pay. There is no argument about that. There is no collective bargaining about that. This does not mean to say, at least I take it does not, that collective bargaining is stopped. Certainly this measure should not bar employees from bargaining if they so choose for an even greater number of days of vacation with pay. However, it does state very definitely that the law shall be that employees shall have two weeks' vacation with pay. I do not think there can be any question about that.
There was a question raised about the regulations. As we all know, it is a fact that regulations must be made under any act, but no regulation at any time can contravene the act itself. All we are concerned about now is the act itself. We cannot debate any of the details of the bill.
