subtopic: PROVISION OP ANNUAL VACATIONS WITH PAY FOR EMPLOYEES IN FEDERAL WORKS
speechtext:
It was
on May 11, 1956 when a bill incorporating the principle of providing vacations with pay for employees under federal jurisdiction was first introduced into this house by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on behalf of the C.C.F. group. I must say that I regret the hon. member is compelled to be away at a time when this bill is being introduced for the first time from the government side.
As has already been made clear by the minister and by others who have participated in the debate, there is a very important difference between the bill introduced in 1956 by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and the bill we now have before us. This difference is that this bill provides for two week's annual vacation with pay only after an employee has completed two years of service rather than after the completion of one year of service as in the former bill. Perhaps one could agree that the action which has come from the government side has arrived a little more quickly than in former years in so far as bills in the field of labour legislation introduced by the C.C.F. group are concerned. This is perhaps the

result of an election which has given us a government who may feel disposed to act a little more quickly than would otherwise have been the case because of the complexion of the membership of the house.
I am quite sure that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) is sincere in his desire to have this legislation become part of the law of Canada. I would suggest, however, he is perhaps adopting some of the practices of his predecessor in office in that he seems disposed to drag his feet considerably in the introduction of certain measures. I would have been much happier if in this bill he had been disposed to go at least as far as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did in 1956. To the working people of Canada it would certainly have appeared that this bill was being brought in with more alacrity than that with which it will appear to have been brought in at the present time. I think that is particularly true because of the fact that it is such a short time since the delegation of the Canadian Labour Congress presented their request to the government for a bill which would provide by law two weeks' vacation with pay after employment for a period of one year.
I must say that I felt the minister's remarks had a familiar ring in respect of the reasons why he was not prepared to go any further than he has gone when he outlined to us the provisions that were existent in the various provincial acts in this same field. He apparently is quite content to stay with that line of argument we used to hear from his predecessor, namely that in the field of labour legislation under no circumstances is the federal government ever to get even half a step ahead of any of the provinces.
Coming as I do from a province where our labour legislation in this field now provides two weeks' vacation after one year of employment, I perhaps am more aware of the fact that the present government is dragging its feet than I would be if I came from one of the other provinces he mentioned where they have not yet any legislation in this field.
In discussing this type of bill previously, I have expressed the point of view that in this field the federal government could very well be the one that was leading the way. We hear a great deal of talk about the need for national unity and for the development of a sense of our Canadian nationhood. I suggest that nothing could help more to create among the working people of Canada that sense of belonging to a Canadian nation than to have a federal government which would be prepared to take a lead in these things as far as its jurisdiction extends. Yet apparently this government, as was the previous government, is prepared to drag its feet and go

only as far as it is pushed by the sheer weight of public opinion as it has expressed itself through the various provincial legislatures.
The minister made reference to some figures with respect to those who now enjoy vacations with pay as far as employees under federal jurisdiction are concerned. If I caught his figures correctly, he said that about
150.000	employees under federal jurisdiction now enjoy two weeks' vacation with pay after three years or more of employment. Those employees, of course, under the bill which he is bringing in, will receive some benefit.
I am interested in the figures he used because of the fact that his predecessor, the former minister of labour, on May 11, 1956, put on Hansard a table indicating the situation in respect of employees under federal labour jurisdiction. According to the figures he gave us at that time, there were about
167.000	employees under federal jurisdiction who were entitled to two weeks' vacation with pay after three years of service. I mention that figure given to us by the former minister of labour and I contrast it with that given today because it indicates that the need which was put forward in 1956 by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre for statutory provision for two weeks' vacation with pay after one year of employment is approximately the same now as it was then.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 27, respecting the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to try to give hon. members of the house the highlights of this bill. There is a lot of background to it. First of all, may I say this is an act respecting the Bell Telephone Company whose main object is that they wish to increase their capital. May I repeat that, Mr. Speaker, they wish to increase their capital.
For the benefit of hon. members who may not have read the bill, the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, which is petitioning for this act, was incorporated by act of parliament on April 29, 1880, just four years after the telephone was invented. At that time there were few scattered telephone companies located in some of the larger cities of eastern Canada, such as Hamilton, London, Windsor, Montreal, Toronto and Quebec. These were purely local systems having a few subscribers, they were not connected with each other. One of the purposes of the incorporation of the Bell Telephone Company of Canada was to bring these small organizations together into one integrated system so as to permit subscribers in one locality to communicate with others in another locality. To this end the Bell Telephone Company of Canada was incorporated with power to extend its operations throughout Canada.
Since the Bell Telephone Company has had to come to the House of Commons to ask for increases in capital due, of course, to increased capital expenditure in line with the growth of Canada and of the telephone service. They came to parliament in 1884; they came again in 1892; they came again in 1902; they came again in 1906; again in 1920, 1929 and 1948; and now, in 1957, they are asking that their capital of $500 million be increased to $1,000 million.
The Bell Telephone Company has, however, never extended its system throughout the whole of Canada. At no time did the company ever operate in British Columbia and in the early years of this century the company had given up its interests in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, and disposed of all

its plant and property in those provinces. The result is that since 1909 the company operations have been confined exclusively to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec with, of course, facilities enabling a connection to be made with the systems serving the other eight provinces and the United States and, either directly or indirectly, connecting with all other systems throughout the world where the interchange of telephone communications is permitted by the laws of other countries and by the facilities provided by such other systems.
Connection may now be had with the systems of 133 other countries. The 2,766,153 telephones which the Bell Telephone Company served at the end of 1956 were all, as I said, located in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Here is just a little history about the percentage of people having telephones. It is estimated that there are about
4,500,000	telephones in Canada, which works out to about one telephone for every four persons. Great Britain has one telephone for every seven people and in the United States there is one telephone for every three people.
Many hon. members may not realize that in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec which the Bell Telephone Company serves there is a total of 677 separate telephone systems. That is just in these two provinces, and it is something a lot of people do not know. The total number of telephones in these provinces is 3,056,000 of which the Bell Telephone Company serves approximately 2,766,000. Of the remaining telephones all but some 300 are served by 674 connecting systems with which the company interchanges service. It is due in great measure to the company's long distance lines that these systems in Ontario and Quebec are interconnected so that a subscriber, as I mentioned before, in one particular district can communicate with a subscriber on another system.
The ratio between telephones and subscribers in the two provinces of Quebec and Ontario is one for every three people. In British Columbia the ratio is also 1 to 3. In Alberta it is 1 to 4; Saskatchewan, 1 to 5; Manitoba, 1 to 4; New Brunswick, 1 to 5; Nova Scotia, 1 to 5; Prince Edward Island, 1 to 7 and Newfoundland 1 to 12. As I said before, in the territory served by the Bell Telephone Company of Canada there is one telephone for every three people. In 1920 there was one telephone for every 10 people.
The Bell Telephone Company is not asking this parliament to vote it the amount of additional capital that it needs. What it asks is that parliament shall grant: first, the

power to create, with the approval of its shareholders, new authorized capital as it needs it to the extent of $500 million; second, the right, having the required authorized capital, to go to the board of transport commissioners for Canada from time to time and try to satisfy it of the propriety of making an issue of a specified amount of such authorized capital and of the price, terms and conditions upon which it is to be issued; and, third, the opportunity, after complying with the applicable securities acts or "blue sky laws", of going to the Canadian investors who, the company believes, have confidence in our country's future and in the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, and seeking from them the capital moneys the company needs for the purpose of serving the public of Ontario and Quebec with essential telephone service.
I have already mentioned the approximate number of telephones which are now in use. Here is something rather interesting: it is estimated that for 1957 there will be 2,980,400 telephones with 2,053,000 subscribers; of course, I suppose a lot of homes have more than one telephone. The number of applications waiting to be dealt with amounts to 18,668 for established services and for a higher grade of service, 38,200, which is over 56,000 unfilled orders. As at the end of 1956 there were 10,276,352 miles of local telephone wire and 1,090,330 miles of long distance telephone wire or a total length of 11,366,682 miles of wire in use. The estimated number of employees at the end of 1957 is 17,300 men and 25,200 women or a total of 42,500 employees.
May I again turn to the petitioner's need for additional capital and point out that at the end of July 31, 1957 it had left $34 million-odd of unissued or uncommitted capital stock. This remaining amount of authorized capital of $34 million-odd is being continually reduced by the monthly issue of shares which have been paid up under the Bell Telephone Company's employee stock plan. The operation of this stock plan will reduce the balance of authorized capital stock to something less than $26 million during the course of next year and $26 million would fall far short of the amount required to enable the company to make an issue of capital stock to provide it with the capital it requires when it next finances by that means. It is wholly insufficient to enable the Bell Telephone Company to carry on its substantial construction program which it now has underway and which it must carry on if the citizens of Ontario and Quebec are to have the telephone service they require and upon which they are dependent to enable them to communicate with citizens in other provinces of Canada, the United States of America and elsewhere in the world.

To provide the telephone facilities required to meet the heavy demand is not just simply a matter of producing telephone instruments and stringing connecting wires. Telephones and wires are useless without switchboards and the central office equipment necessary to make them function. Switchboards and central office equipment are most complicated pieces of apparatus. They cannot be obtained ready made and must be designed and manufactured for the precise place in which they are to be installed. Then too, the company cannot instal switchboards and central office equipment without having proper buildings in which to house them. These buildings and additions to buildings must be designed and erected. It will be appreciated that the planning, designing, manufacturing and erection of switchboards and central office equipment and buildings all involve projects which must be planned in advance, engineer designed and provided very far in advance of when required to provide time to carry them into effect. It will also be appreciated that in the planning and designing of equipment and buildings it is necessary for the company to be in a position where it can see its way clear to finance such projects. It is unthinkable that the company should let itself, or be permitted, to run out of the funds required for providing and extending service to the people of Canada.
Some hon. members may wonder what the company is going to do with this additional capital if it is allowed to increase and dispose of it. The company estimates that in the next five years, commencing in 1958, it will have the following construction expenditures: $191 million, $204 million, $197 million, $189 million and $181 million or a total of $962 million. Some hon. members might also ask where the company will get the extra $462 million. The company feels that with the increase in capital it will be able to use its assets for borrowing the balance and thus, with an increase in capital of $500 million, it plans to spend $962 million within the next five years commencing, as I said, in 1958.
I have given a breakdown of the company's estimated construction expenditures. The company figures it will have to pay $1 million for rights of way, $66 million for lands and buildings, $339 million for central office equipment, $236 million for station equipment, $281 million for outside plant and $39 million for general equipment.
Figures are sometimes rather pleasant to hear and I have some additional calculations which may interest hon. members. In 1947 the company handled 165,000 long distance calls every day and in 1956 it handled
317,000	long distance calls each day. In 1956

Private Bills
the company handled a combined total oi local and long distance calls of 18 million a day. There must be a lot of talking done in this country and I am sure all of it is not done on the floor of this house.
I might advise hon. members that this bill will go to the appropriate committee so that if hon. members wish to ask technical questions they will have the opportunity of addressing them to officials of the Bell Telephone Company who will be present to answer them. I take pleasure, Mr. Speaker, in moving second reading of this bill.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest to the recital of the history and accomplishments and purposes of this company by the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill. I judge that the document was carefully prepared by the solicitors of the company because it read in quite a legal form.
This is a very important bill. We have here a private corporation coming to this house asking for permission to increase its capital by $500 million. As a matter of fact, this bill provides for a billion dollar development by a private company over which this house has very little control. Now, I would not deny the necessity for the extension of the services rendered by this company in that portion of Canada it serves but this is a tremendous expansion by a private monopoly largely owned and controlled in the United States, and while the telephones are located in Ontario the ownership and control is located south of the border.
A search of the records of the combines investigation branch, in this house and in other places, and a reading of the history of monopolies in Canada will provide illustrations of many unsavoury developments and incidents. The whole history of combines development in this country is marked with unethical practices. We had that brought to our attention just the other day by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) in his announcement to the house with respect to the intended prosecution of a supposed combine in this country. One has only to read the records of the past of the comparatively small number of investigations and prosecutions in relation to the number of combines that exist in Canada to realize that this type of development, in the opinion of this group and in the opinion of an increasing number of people in this country is not in the interests of the Canadian people. It is no wonder that increasing numbers of the public are becoming suspicious of the large scale development of these monopolies. We all know that recent disclosures with respect to the control of pipe line companies, their financing and the

profits made by a very few individuals, which the consumers of this country will have to pay, are increasing that concern and causing it to grow from day to day.
I tell you, Mr. Speaker, I am normally a very placid and mild mannered man but I am surprised at the letters I receive from people, who are even supporters of the government party in this house, expressing concern over this developing control of our economy by very few individuals. This is also indicated by editorials in the press across this country. One has only to read the Free Press of recent date, the Toronto Telegram, I think it was, and the Vancouver Sun, to realize that even these orthodox papers are becoming conscious of public opinion in this respect and are reflecting public opinion to the extent that they deal with this question. The combinations that are developing in the transportation of gas, oil and other public services and the development of our natural resources are causing the promotion of larger and larger combines of capital and are handing the actual control of this nation over to fewer and fewer people.
What about this company? I do not blame individuals. After all, we are creatures of the environment in which we live. I think we in this House of Commons are sent here to express our opinions and to express them fairly and clearly when we see situations developing, as a result of the rather better opportunities we have than the average Canadian citizen has to see how these things are developing. What about this company? Outside of obtaining a licence from the board of transport commissioners and the reference as to rates, there is actually no other control over this company. So far as services are concerned, this company can do exactly as the British Columbia Telephone Company does, carry on its extensions and developments according to its own desires and its own wishes and give service where it is profitable and deny it where it is not. I do not think that is a proper situation, Mr. Speaker.
No doubt when the present legislation was first introduced it was satisfactory because there were relatively few large corporations in this country and monopoly development had not gone to the stage that it has today. However, we are living in changing times and circumstances and I suggest we have to use new procedures to meet those changing times and circumstances if we are to make certain that these developments are to the advantage of the people as a whole. Therefore, I am going to make a suggestion, and I am not for one moment suggesting that it is an original thought with me. I think it is

time that we had a committee of this house and of the Senate to inquire into the activities and effects of public service corporations which are monopolies in this country.
In this house we have an opportunity periodically to examine the operations of the nationally-owned railroads. That is done in a committee of the house. We have an opportunity to examine the banks, but once this company obtains its licence and its rates are established by the board of transport commissioners there is no control, no planning and no direction. These financial groups are carrying on in that way. As I said before, I do not blame any individual but I think it is about time that a committee of this house, in association with members of the Senate, had the opportunity to make a thorough investigation of the activities and the effects of these large public service corporations which are monopolies.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is about time that the people knew the facts and this is one way to obtain the facts which hon. members should take advantage of and exercise some increasing control over these large corporations and monopolies through this house which represents the people.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a bill which affects Ontario and Quebec, I think, more than it does any other part of Canada. I have not had time to go over it too carefully. It is a rather complicated bill. Our experience in the past when dealing with subjects of this kind, has indicated that there should be a good deal of careful thought and study before this house gives its consent to such a measure as this. Last year we had the experience of a pipe line company which wanted to divide its shares five for one. On the surface there did not seem to be much objection to it. I took the stand on that occasion that we would not give our consent to the passing of the bill until it had a thorough going over in the committee and after that had been done we would be in a better position to give our decision as to whether or not we favoured the bill. I think the same thing could be true here.
This is a large company. Of course, I am not objecting on the ground that it is a large company, as the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) did, and certainly not for the same reasons he gave; but I think we should be careful with a bill such as this one before we pass judgment on it.
The sponsor has stated that it is going to the committee. Since he has said that it is not necessary for me to dwell too long on the bill because my experience has been that
Private Bills
when a bill of this kind gets before the committee and the proper witnesses are called that is the time and place when all these different details can be brought out.
On the surface, it seems to me a rather large order for this company to come here and ask permission to double its capitalization, and especially when it wants the right to raise its capital another $500 million from time to time without coming to the house for consent.
I have never known the house on any occasion, when there was a bill of this kind put before it and the reasons were legitimate and it was supposed to be in the interests of Canada, not to give consent. It does seem to me a pretty big order when they say that the company shall increase its capital assets from time to time without having to come back to the House of Commons. In view of the fact that it is a rather large order to ask for we should be a little cautious and at least the members of this house and of the committee should go into it very carefully.
As I say, the hon. member has indicated that the bill is to go to a committee. I am going to leave my reservations at that; I am not going to commit myself one way or the other on this bill, whether we will give our consent to it or not, until we have had it before the committee and there decided on its merits.

subtopic: THE BELL TELEPHONE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the request in this bill the Bell Telephone Company of Canada, with control from the other side, is coming to the government and asking permission to expand its capital assets by another $500 million. That is quite a heavy order. It is becoming a rather powerful company.
The member who is sponsoring the bill indicated this afternoon that the company is going to do some expansion in the way of providing telephone service to the people of Ontario and Quebec. There is a great demand for such service and I am sure that these people would like to see telephones installed in their homes as quickly as possible so that they may receive service. But surely it would not require this amount of money to provide these services for the people of these two provinces.
As a matter of fact I believe that behind the bill is a plan to get control of a much larger field of communications than simply telephone service and not only within two provinces. I believe their aim is nationwide control in some fields of communication which are very important to us. When the president of this company dealt with the matter in a speech about a year ago, as reported in the Financial Post, he indicated a much wider and broader field of expansion

Private Bills
than presented this afternoon by the hon. member who is sponsoring the bill. The president of the company indicated pretty clearly what their plans were. He told about what the company was doing in the expansion of what they called the picture-phone. The company's laboratories are now working on a project whereby when you telephone someone and they answer a picture will appear and you will be able to see the person to whom you are speaking.
There is also expansion in the field of long distance dialing. Those who use the long distance services can verify that very quick service is given by means of long distance dialing. Operators in one city can dial almost directly through to other cities in different parts of Canada and give very rapid service.
There is also rapid development in the teletype field and in what the company calls integrated data processing whereby business machinery in an office in one part of the country is connected with mobile radio installations and central control agencies and can receive signals from other offices of the business throughout the whole of Canada. The example the president of the company used at that time to illustrate the company's intentions was the trans-Canada pipe line. When the line is finally in operation the central control office of the company is going to require immediate data respecting the flow in various parts of the 2,000 mile pipe line. This is an excellent project and shows remarkable progress.
The president of the company referred to another field which the hon. member did not mention at all this afternoon, the rapid expansion of control by this company of the whole microwave relay system across Canada which will extend from Sydney, Noya Scotia, to Vancouver. The telephone company has already built most of the system and by the end of next year they expect to have the microwave relay stations completed. It will be a billion dollar operation before final construction is completed.
What I should like to draw to the attention of hon. members and warn them about is the fact that once this company gets this amount of money, proceeds to expand and and is given the right to control the microwave relay field, practically every television station across Canada will have to rent the service of the Bell Telephone Company in Order to secure transmission of television programs. The president also stated that the company would have facilities for colour television. I should like to know the extent to which the C.B.C. is renting the service of the Bell Telephone Company microwave relay system: for their broadcasts at the

present time. What is the tribute being paid by the C.B.C. to the Bell Telephone Company today? What is going to be the position of the Bell Telephone Company in another ten years with regard to complete control of the microwave relay system? When it is estab-listed they can quite readily and easily prevent any competition of any kind. They will remove competition from the field. If they remove competition from the field, then what is the toll the Canadian people will have to pay for the operation of the telephone company's television relay and communication systems throughout the country?
If private enterprise can carry out this project, let it do so, but everyone who supports the private enterprise idea states that one of the main objectives, one of the things which keeps private enterprise on the go, is competition. What happens when you eliminate competition? Is there any possibility of competition in this most important field? Communications are vital to modern industry and modern living. Does this bill mean that the company is going to have a monopoly in the television microwave relay field throughout the country? If it does, then I think we should oppose it.
My reason for saying that is that when competition is not possible we have a system of guarantee extortion from the Canadian people, and I do not believe our people will support the granting of monopoly in a public service to any company. To prevent that kind of thing, we believe it is a good idea for the government to go into the public service field. If there are any profits to be made from that field, then those profits will accrue to all the Canadian people rather than one powerful, wealthy firm being permitted to have control and name its price for its services.
In the province from which I come, and a number of the western provinces are the same, the telephone service has never been a private enterprise concern. Telephone communication is considered a public service. We have a government telephone service, in my opinion the best service in Canada. I might say that the profit motive is not the only thing involved there. I think the province of Saskatchewan is the only one where local telephone calls through pay telephones still only cost a nickle. Every place else it is 10 cents.
There is another field I should like to look into here. To what extent are the rights of a province respecting communications within its boundaries protected? Can we guarantee that each province that wishes to maintain control Of , its own communications will be

protected and that it will not be affected adversely by agreement or otherwise or through lack of service because it did not wish to pay a toll to this giant corporation for communications throughout the province? Surely the province has certain rights, and I hope they will be protected. I hope that when the bill goes to the committee the members who will investigate the company and ask questions will make very sure that the rights of the provinces are not interfered with in any way.
The provincial governments are watching the situation very carefully. I know that my own province of Saskatchewan has made arrangements for the use of the microwave system. They are using the microwave facilities and are connected with the long distance services of other communication systems across the dominion by means of arrangements and agreements. I want to see that these things are maintained and that nothing harmful will be done in the future.
I do not wish to frown on private enterprise where it is providing a service but I do frown on private enterprise when it becomes a monopoly. I do not think the actions of this or any other government or anything that we do in this house should in any way lead to the establishment of a monopoly in a public service, something which is essential to civilization as we know it. With these safeguards, I would be glad to see this bill passed, go to the committee and when it comes back it will have our blessing. Without these assurances, Mr. Speaker, I can assure you that I and others in this group will oppose it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) I may say that this bill has nothing to do with increases in rates at all. It only has to do with an increase in the capital stock of the Bell Telephone Company.
Private Bills
The hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Castle-den) talked about the lack of control. May I remind him that this company is under the jurisdiction and control of the board of transport commissioners. This board has very wide powers. They can, from time to time, as the occasion may arise, review, rescind, change, alter or vary their own decisions. They have power and jurisdiction over all requirements under the company's special act; any agreements the company enters into; to make inquiries into the company's operations; to inspect the company's work; to regulate the construction of the company's work when matters of public safety are involved, for example as at railway crossings. The board can order the company to make repairs; they regulate the company's tolls and tariffs.
The board of transport commissioners regulates the company's rates; regulates joint tariffs. They have jurisdiction over the publication of tariffs; over contracts to limit liability; over construction of lines upon or across highways; over construction of lines across other lines; over construction of the company's lines with the lines of other systems; over all contracts the company makes with other telephone systems and subscribers. They have the right to inquire into any contract whatsoever into which the company may enter. Also, as I mentioned before, the Bell Telephone Company shall not have the power to make any issue, sale or other disposition of its capital stock without first obtaining the approval of the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada of the amount, terms and conditions of such issue, sale or other disposition of such capital stock.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a bill which will inaugurate a free enterprise which I think will be more palatable to my friends across the way in that it is concerned with selling the idea of savings to the people of Canada. This, of course, as they will agree, is of an anti-inflationary nature which accrues to the benefit of us all in a country of this nature. As our time is short, for the benefit of this house I shall read the history of the company sponsoring this bill, namely Investors Syndicate of Canada Limited.

Private Bills
The Investors Syndicate originated in the United States before the turn of the century. There was a Minnesota company called Investors Syndicate. It was owned by Investors Diversified Holding Company. That company in Minnesota started doing business in western Canada, under the firm name and style of Investors Syndicate of the United States. They started business in the twenties and they sold here in Canada the same form of investment contracts that they sold in the States. They are contracts where the purchaser names the term at the end of which he desires to provide for himself a lump sum of money, in consideration for which he can arrange either for part, or a stipulated payment, and they invest these moneys, generally in mortgages, and have done so very successfully. They are cash values and form a sinking fund.
In 1940 they decided that it would be better if they had a Canadian company, so they obtained a special act in Manitoba in 1940 incorporating Investors Syndicate Limited of Canada, being chapter 88 of the statutes of Manitoba, 1940. As pointed out previously, the Canadian company was still owned by the Investors Diversified Services Incorporated. They have over $1 million in assets now. They continued to sell investment contracts providing a stipulated sum at the end of a specified term.
The so-called Investors Mutual of Canada Limited was incorporated in 1948. It has assets of $150 million. Since 1950 it has become the largest mutual investors fund in Canada, even greater than the Canadian Investors Fund. The assets of Investors Syndicate are largely formed of mortgages, about 75 per cent, and the rest in bonds. The assets of Investors Mutual are all in bonds and stocks, with hundreds of millions of assets.
The third company was incorporated this year and was called the Investors Growth Fund Limited. The purpose of this new company was to have a separate mutual investment in which the assets would be invested solely in common stock.
As already mentioned, the Investors Syndicate consists of principally mortgages, a few bonds and even fewer stocks; the Investors Mutual consists of bonds and stocks, no mortgages; and the Investors Growth Fund consists of nothing but stocks, preferred and common.
In 1956 they concluded, with the growth of their business in Canada, that it would be better still if it were controlled in Canada rather than still controlled by the holding company in the United States, namely Investors Diversified Services Incorporated. In 1956 they issued additional stock in Investors
[Mr. Chown.l
Syndicate of Canada and they increased it to the same number of shares as the holding company had outstanding and then they issued these shares to the individual shareholders in the United States and Canada.
The ownership of Investors Syndicate of Canada was transferred from the holding company in the United States to the individuals in the United States and Canada of which there were many. Many of the individuals in the United States in turn sold their shares to Canadians, with the result that many of the shares are now controlled and owned, to the extent of 75 per cent to 80 per cent, by Canadians.
Why do they want the trust company now? They do not intend to engage in most of the usual fields of trust companies. They do not intend to administer estates. They do not intend to look after cash deposits or trust funds. Their reasons for wanting a trust company are: One, to enable the trust company to manage a group pension plan for employers who desire to run their own plans rather than to place them with insurance companies; two, to take full advantage of the amendment to the Income Tax Act under section 79 (b), both for employers and selfemployed.
Their form of investment is mostly mortgage. They want to be in a position to compete with other trust companies. It is correct to say that the trust company is not seeking any special powers but only powers comparable with the trust companies in the pension field. As they wish to look after personal investments, they must be a trust company under Dominion statute.
Under clause 5, the company shall not commence business until at least $1 million of its capital has been subscribed to and paid for. Under clause 6, the company acquires the same powers as any company under the Trust Company Model Act. Therefore by this act they can go into other trust company fields in estates or deposits, if they so desire, at a future date.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, the sponsoring company, namely Investors Syndicate Canada Limited, is now 75 per cent to 80 per cent Canadian owned. The objects of Investors Syndicate and its existing subsidiaries, Investors Mutual Limited and the Investors Growth Fund Limited, are to encourage Canadians to save something which of itself is an anti-inflationary objective. Now they want to incorporate this company to be known as Investors Trust Company so that they can operate in another aspect of the field which has as its objective plans for saving money.
It is my privilege to know the president of Investors Syndicate and many of the other

officers of this company and of its existing subsidiaries. They are all of the highest integrity and greatly respected by their friends and their competitors across the nation. For this reason I have no hesitation in asking this house to assent to the second reading of this bill.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.
